Atoms to Processes: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Chemical Engineering

Abstract

The rapid maturation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has catalyzed a profound shift in how chemical engineering problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. Advances in computing, data availability, and learning algorithms have enabled AI/ML methods to impact applications spanning atomic-scale simulations, materials and catalyst discovery, transport and thermodynamics, separations, process systems engineering, and industrial operations. This article provides a perspective on recent methodological developments and representative applications, emphasizing how AI/ML tools are being integrated with first-principles models to address challenges of predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation, interpretability, and model lifecycle management.

Across domains, a unifying trend is the move away from purely black-box approaches toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks that explicitly respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and known structural constraints. These approaches not only improve robustness and reliability, but also enable meaningful human–AI collaboration by providing information at an appropriate level of abstraction for the task and decision context. We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise will be essential to realizing their full potential across both research and industrial practice.

1 Introduction

The adoption of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) tools and methods in chemical engineering research and applications has been under discussion since at least the 1990s. However, widespread translation of these methods into industrial practice did not occur in the subsequent decades. Venkatasubramanian 1 identified several contributing factors: the intrinsic difficulty of many problems, the availability of satisfactory solutions through conventional approaches, and the limited computational capabilities of the time. Further difficulties came from the fact that many ML/AI methods inherently require large amounts of data for model training and validation.

Since then, the substantial advance in computing power (boosted by specialized hardware such as GPUs), data acquisition and storage, coupled with the capacity to train large-scale ML models, have enabled transformative progress across diverse domains, including e-commerce, computer vision, natural language processing, and, more recently, generative AI.

In the scientific and engineering context, high throughput experimentation as well as new modeling and computation tools accelerated the generation of data, and ML/AI tools have already demonstrated utility in applications such as catalyst discovery and prediction of physicochemical properties of organic molecules.

The effective deployment of ML and AI models in science and engineering requires careful attention to several specific considerations. First, predictive accuracy is paramount. For example, errors in predicting the viscosity of a novel molecule at the computational design stage could produce a solid at the synthesis stage, whereas the target was a liquid material. At the process level, overestimation of product purity may result in the production of off-specification material and associated penalties, while underestimation may yield unnecessarily high-purity product and associated revenue loss. In this context, it can be equally important to quantify the uncertainty associated with model predictions, as awareness of prediction confidence can guide decision-making, risk mitigation, and additional validation. In the above example, a model predicting a liquid with high uncertainty might trigger further validation before synthesis.

Second, ML models must remain consistent with physical laws, as the data on which they are trained represent physical systems constrained by mass and energy conservation laws. Third, models should exhibit a degree of interpretability, allowing their behavior to be understood in relation to the governing equations and principles of the underlying system. Fourth, interpretability should allow for transfer learning, or the ability of a model to represent systems that are physically/structurally similar to those whose data it was trained on, potentially with some amount of fine tuning. This is essentially an extrapolation capacity. Fifth, model maintenance is essential. Thinking particularly at the macroscopic scale, industrial plants evolve continuously: equipment replacement, catalyst deactivation, corrosion, and fouling all lead to gradual deviations between model predictions and plant performance. Accordingly, models must be updated regularly to mitigate prediction drift.

Last but not least, reproducibility is a precondition for all of the above, yet it remains one of the field’s most persistent and under-addressed weaknesses. Reported model performance can be verified, compared fairly across studies, or built upon only when the underlying computational workflow is fully disclosed and re-runnable. In practice, chemical engineering AI/ML publications routinely omit one or more of the following: source code, data preprocessing and featurization scripts, the exact train/validation/test splits, trained model weights, hyperparameter settings and the search procedure used to obtain them, random seeds, and the software and library versions needed to regenerate results. The absence of these materials has repeatedly forced researchers to spend substantial effort reimplementing or guessing at published workflows, and it makes it difficult to distinguish genuine methodological advances from artifacts of undisclosed data splits, tuning budgets, or preprocessing choices. Adjacent computational disciplines and journals, e.g., the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, have moved toward explicit minimum reproducibility requirements for computational submissions. We argue that chemical engineering AI/ML research, and the journals and venues that publish it, should move toward comparable, explicitly stated minimum standards for code and data availability and computational reproducibility.

This contribution outlines the open challenges associated with these requirements and discusses promising avenues for advancing the application of AI and ML in chemical engineering. Following a high-level overview of recent relevant methodological developments, we organize the paper along the sections of Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research (I&ECR).

2 Engineering-Relevant AI/ML Methodology

The developments and challenges reviewed above emphasize the breadth and diversity of problems encountered across chemical engineering, which has naturally led to the adoption of a broad range of AI and ML methods. These methods differ in how they utilize data, incorporate domain/physical knowledge, and balance interpretability with predictive power.

The development of AI and ML models often begins with careful formulation of the learning task: regression or classification for property prediction, sequence modeling for time-series plant data, or generative modeling for molecular and process design. A critical first step involves representing chemical and engineering data and domain knowledge as mathematical inputs. Examples include structured fingerprints or graph representations for molecules, topology- or string-based representations for reactions, and digitized process flowsheets for plant models 2, 3. Data reconciliation is a common step in engineering because raw data may violate mass/energy balances, contain noise, or reflect operating constraints that must be preserved.

Below, we highlight several methodological classes that have proven particularly relevant to chemical engineering applications (Figure 1).

2.1 Classical Supervised Learning: Regression, Forecasting, and Classification

Supervised learning remains the dominant paradigm for chemical engineering applications of AI. In this setting, models are trained on labeled data pairs to predict either continuous outputs (regression) or discrete labels (classification). This setting occurs in property prediction, surrogate modeling of high-fidelity simulations, and general modeling of experimental data. Classification algorithms are commonly employed for fault detection and diagnosis, quality monitoring, and operating-regime identification 4. Regression models range from simple, e.g., linear and kernel-based approaches, to deep neural networks, reflecting a trade-off between expressivity, interpretability, and data requirements 3. Linear and generalized linear models remain widely used because they offer mechanistic interpretability and naturally align with many engineering correlations, especially when the input features are designed strategically 5.

Kernel-based methods and support vector machines provide nonlinear modeling capacity while remaining simple in form, making them effective for the moderate data volumes found in experimental areas. Ensemble methods, such as random forests and gradient boosting, can offer improved accuracy without significant additional model design. The advent of neural networks and deep learning architectures, including fully connected networks, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks, saw a significant increase in chemical engineering applications, spanning molecular, material, and process scales. Methodologically, while deep learning models can be universal approximators, a significant challenge in chemical and engineering applications is controlling overfitting with limited data 6; several paradigms are used to mitigate this risk, including regularization terms 7, judicious architecture design 8, data augmentation 9, and hybrid modeling 10.

Of the above, hybrid modeling has seen a particular focus in the literature 11. Chemical engineering data obey physical laws, e.g., mass and energy conservation, thermodynamic constraints, kinetic rate laws, and known symmetries. Hybrid models seek to integrate data-driven models within these first-principles equations, e.g., using ML to estimate unknown relationships, refine thermodynamic or kinetic parameters, or provide corrections to the outputs of mechanistic simulators 10. These approaches maintain and incorporate known physical knowledge while allowing the data-driven component to approximate unknown relationships between the input variables, producing models that are more interpretable and better behaved under extrapolation than purely black-box learners. For many chemical engineering tasks, hybrid supervised learning represents a promising compromise between empirical correlations and fully data-driven models. More recently, “physics-informed” ML approaches embed physical structure or relationships directly into architectures or loss functions. Methodologies here include designing model connectivity based on known relationships 12, including physics-based penalties, such as governing equations and/or optimality conditions, during training 13, 14, 15, 16, and physics-based feature engineering 17. In general, these inductive biases help restrict the space of model parameters to be physically feasible, improving model performance, as well as interpretability and extrapolation safety.

A subfield of supervised learning focuses on forecasting, or making predictions based on historical time-series data. Building these “dynamical system” models (i.e., system identification), is a classical area of study in the field of process control, leading to methods such as state-space models, Hammerstein–Wiener models, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models. These classical models are relatively compact and amenable to deployment in linear model predictive control 18, nonlinear control 19, and optimization-based scheduling 20. More recent work has focused on deep-learning forecasting models, such as recurrent neural networks and transformer models, which are capable of learning more complex dynamics, such as unknown reaction pathways 21 and crystallization kinetics 22. Finally, an orthogonal line of research has sought dynamic symbolic models, providing interpretability and potentially helping uncover mechanistic equations directly from data 23, 24.

2.2 Active Learning and Reinforcement Learning

Data are often expensive to generate, whether from process operations, bench-scale experiments, or computational simulations 6. Active learning seeks to maximize information gain from limited data acquisition by iteratively selecting new samples where the model uncertainty is highest. Traditional approaches relied on model-based design of experiments 25, system identification, or dual control. More recently, ML- and AI-based design-of-experiments (DoE) have demonstrated promise in materials discovery, reaction optimization, and process calibration, where automated and autonomous experimental platforms can reduce both cost and time 26. A particularly influential class of algorithms here is Bayesian optimization (BO), which views experiment design from the lens of global optimization of an expensive black-box function 27, 28. BO couples a probabilistic ML model with an acquisition function that quantifies the value of experiments, i.e., to balance exploration and exploitation 29. To tackle chemical engineering challenges, methodological advances have sought to integrate BO in high-dimensional or hybrid (discrete/continuous) variable settings 6, BO with multi-fidelity data (e.g., combining experiments and simulations) 30, and BO with hybrid, grey-box models 31, enabling more reliable optimization when training data are sparse or partially simulated.

Whereas active learning focuses on data acquisition, a separate paradigm, reinforcement learning (RL) addresses the problem of sequential decision-making. In RL, an agent learns optimal control strategies directly through interaction with an environment. This formulation naturally aligns with process systems engineering challenges, including control, scheduling, adaptive experimentation, and process optimization tasks 32, 33. In particular, modern deep RL algorithms (e.g., deep deterministic policy gradients, proximal policy optimization) provide increasing levels of model complexity and flexibility for nonlinear, high-dimensional chemical engineering systems 34. Nevertheless, exploration is often hazardous or impractical in these applications, motivating the use of hybrid RL strategies. Two main paradigms have emerged here: (1) learning from simulated data, reduced-order models, or off-policy data from an expert controller 35, 36, and (2) hybrid frameworks integrating physical knowledge, constraints, or controllers to enforce safe behavior 37, 38, 39.

2.3 Unsupervised Learning: Dimensionality Reduction and Embeddings

Unsupervised learning methods uncover underlying structure (i.e., a subspace) in high-dimensional data without requiring labeled outputs and are central to multivariate process monitoring in chemical engineering. Classical latent-variable methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) and its (dynamic) extensions can project correlated process or spectroscopy data for later ML applications, e.g., soft sensors 40, 41, 42. More recent works apply ML models such as autoencoders, variational autoencoders (VAEs), and geometric manifold learning techniques to learn more complex latent spaces underlying data. At the molecular and materials scale, representation learning plays an analogous role. Variational autoencoders and related models learn continuous molecular embeddings to define chemically similar molecules 43; this has enabled inverse materials design workflows by optimizing in continuous latent space and decoding to valid structures 44, 45.

2.4 Generative Modeling and Foundation Models

Generative models learn mappings from low-dimensional latent spaces to distributions over molecules, materials, or process systems, thereby shifting the focus from prediction to design. This is essentially the inverse task of prediction models: sampling candidates that satisfy desired properties rather than predicting properties. For example, the above studies 44, 45 use VAEs for molecular design, while Yue et al. 46 provide a benchmarking comparison of generative models for polymer design. Following the advances in the ML and AI fields, more complex models such as GPT- and diffusion-based models are recently employed for similar generative tasks, e.g., in polymer design 47 and process flowsheeting 48.

In parallel, the emergence of foundation models, i.e., large, pre-trained architectures adaptable to downstream tasks, has begun to reshape workflows across chemical engineering fields. Within foundation models, a particular focus has been large language models (LLMs), or pre-trained models on natural language that can directly be used, e.g., for documentation and education tasks 49. Many recent works adapt LLMs to the “language” of chemical engineering, potentially accelerating the pace of discovery 50, 51. Specialized models such as Molformer 52 and Chemformer 53 provide foundation models pre-trained for chemistry-related tasks, while tabular foundation models 54, 55 leverage in-context learning to make predictions using small datasets (characteristic of many chemical engineering problems) without task-specific training.

Beyond passive generation, recent work also explores tool-augmented and agentic AI systems, in which foundation models are coupled with external tools such as process simulators, optimization routines, and scientific databases to iteratively solve complex tasks. In this paradigm, large language models (LLMs) can orchestrate complex, multi-step workflows by generating inputs to simulation environments, invoking property prediction models, or querying experimental data 56, 57. Predictions can be improved based on returned results, inter-agent coordination, and/or interaction with the human user. Early demonstrations include automated drug discovery and materials design 58, 59, control and operational decision-making 60, 61, and process design and simulation 62, 63. While still emerging, this direction is particularly relevant to chemical engineering, where established first-principles models and simulation environments provide a natural interface for hybrid, AI-driven decision-making systems that bridge data-driven and physics-based approaches.

3 Kinetics, Catalysis and Reaction Engineering

Kinetics, catalysis, and reaction engineering have been significantly influenced by ML and AI models in recent years. The use of ML in catalysis dates back to the early days of ML and AI in chemical engineering, and these early impacts are reviewed elsewhere64. More recently, ML models have become ubiquitous in the field of computational catalysis, where atomic-scale and microkinetic models are used to understand and predict catalytic materials. In addition, ML models have been used extensively in conjunction with or in place of traditional optimization techniques to extract kinetic equations and rate parameters from data measured using real or simulated chemical reactors. Finally, ML and AI models have been heavily used to discover and optimize catalyst formulations, replacing or augmenting traditional “quantitative structure-property relationships” and accelerating high-throughput computational and experimental screening. Here, we briefly review some recent representative examples of each area, focusing on primary sources.

3.1 Simulations of catalysts and kinetic processes

3.1.1 Atomic-scale simulations of active sites and surfaces

The use of atomic-scale models to understand catalytic processes is a common strategy in the field, and has historically been achieved using density functional theory (DFT), which captures covalent bonding effects critical to catalysis, but is fast enough to be applied to surface slabs commonly used to model solid/liquid or solid/gas interfaces (see, e.g., 65). Even though DFT is faster than other quantum-mechanical methods, it is still far too slow for realistic catalyst particles or for the large-scale sampling needed for statistical-mechanical analyses. The advent of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) has been transformative to the field of computational catalysis, as they provide accuracies comparable to DFT (∼0.2\sim 0.2–0.50.5 eV errors on adsorption energies) at speeds thousands of times faster than DFT (e.g., 66). Combining these MLIPs with DFT through active learning has become ubiquitous in the field of computational catalysis, and is now widely used to accelerate common tasks like geometry optimizations and transition-state searches (e.g., 67, 68). One notable example is AdsorbDiff, which uses a generative diffusion model to directly predict adsorbate configurations 69. In addition, MLIPs have been used in conjunction with DFT to find global minima of various types of adsorbates and active sites 70, 71, 72, a task that is computationally intractable with DFT alone. Moreover, MLIPs have enabled substantial advances in the statistical sampling of potential energy surfaces of adsorbed species, providing a route to compute more accurate entropies and free energies of adsorption and activation 73, 74. Finally, MLIPs have drastically increased the length scales that are accessible in catalytic simulations, making it possible to model entire supported nanoparticles 75 or micron-scale surfaces 76. These AI and ML capabilities have substantially improved the complexity of active site models and the accuracy of surface reaction free energies that are critical to bottom-up simulations of catalyst surfaces. However, it is worth considering some existing limitations of MLIPs. These approaches are only ever capable of reproducing the accuracy of the underlying electronic structure methods used to generate training data, and even these methods are known to suffer from accuracy limitations 77. Moreover, validation of long timescale simulations with MLIPs is difficult, since it is not possible to re-run the full simulation at DFT-level fidelity. Spot checks along the trajectory are often used to assess validity, and active learning schemes can be used to combine MLIPs with DFT to improve accuracy 78, 67, 68. Uncertainty quantification for MLIPs is an emerging area of interest, although assessing the quality of uncertainty estimates is challenging, especially outside the training domain 79, 80, 81, 82. Nonetheless, MLIPs are one of the most impactful AI/ML developments in computational materials science and catalysis 66, 83, 84.

3.1.2 Identification of reaction networks and mechanisms

Beyond active sites, it is also critical to consider reaction networks when modeling catalytic reactions. Chemistries of interest in kinetics and catalysis typically consist of thousands of reactions and species, particularly when reactive intermediates are included. If simulations of the complex chemistry of thermal and catalytic processes are to be carried out with high fidelity, it is critical that tools for the generation of mechanisms, active sites and microkinetic models be developed and applied, which is the purview of AI and ML. Early efforts trace back to the 1970s, in which computers were armed with information about patterns of reactivity, now referred to template-based approaches, gleaned from experts and organic chemistry textbooks, an early form of AI. Various groups have developed software for mechanism generation over the years (e.g., 85, 86), and a network or mechanism generator has become an essential part of a kinetic modeler’s toolbox (e.g., 87). The earliest AI tools for mechanism generation focused on homogeneous chemistries such as pyrolysis and combustion, but more recent efforts have tackled the complexity engendered by a catalytic surface, active sites and adsorbates. In the realm of generating complex reaction networks for reactions on heterogeneous catalysts, recent examples include RMG-Cat 88 and Genesys-Cat 89. RMG-Cat iteratively proposes new reactions according to reaction templates, but it includes only the reactions that are kinetically significant based on a precompiled database of thermodynamic properties and rate coefficients for known species and reactions, along with the ability to estimate these parameters for new species and reactions. To validate it, the authors showed that it successfully “discovered” many of the same reactions as a previously compiled mechanism that was developed over many years by experts for an example reaction system. Genesys-Cat operates in a similar fashion, functioning as both a model generator that can generate gas- and surface-phase mechanisms in parallel, which are compatible with standard packages such as Chemkin and Cantera, demonstrated well on catalytic cracking of iso-octane for three different zeolites but also being applicable to conventional metal catalysts. A challenge that arises for reactions on heterogeneous catalytic surfaces, however, is determining where adsorbates bind and how neighboring adsorbed molecules affect their adsorption kinetics and thermodynamics. Kolluru and Kitchen address this challenge with machine learning 69, which not only provides guidance for development of microkinetic models for a given catalytic surface or facet, but also allows for high throughput evaluation. As the authors note, the quest for the lowest energy adsorbed geometries has relied on heuristics, problem-specific intuitions, or brute-force approaches to guide adsorbate placement. Instead, they propose a novel framework for adsorbate placement using denoising diffusion which includes optimization with a pretrained machine learning force field, the output of which can be analyzed using density functional theory.

Estimation of rate coefficients remains the most significant challenge of complex kinetic modeling, as a rate coefficient must be estimated for every elementary step reaction, adsorbate configuration, surface facet, and active site. Here again, though, ML is being deployed to great benefit. As a recent example, Zhang et al. 90 studied intramolecular H-migration in ether peroxy radicals, species that are relevant to low-temperature combustion. A machine learning framework was developed based on two topological descriptors, capturing reactant topology, and five reaction-specific descriptors, characterizing reaction center properties, to estimate rate coefficients. It was shown that the ML model outperformed rate rule approaches, particularly for cases that were not easily generalizable, with significantly enhanced computational efficiency. Shi et al. 91 showed similar success with a ML model used to predict rate coefficients for the interaction of ozone with various organic contaminants. While the ML models were not readily interpreted mechanistically, their practical application and ability to fit well with workflows focusing on complex mechanism generation are notable. This was also the focus of the work of Liu et al. 92, who proposed a framework that employs ML to accelerate the analysis of chemical reaction networks for complex gas-phase reaction systems. In addition to using ML to estimate rate coefficients, associated prediction uncertainties of reactions within the chemical systems and influential reactions with high-level uncertainty of predicted rate constants are identified.

3.2 Treatment of coverage effects in kinetic models

Another area where AI and ML models are having a growing impact on kinetic modeling is in the treatment of lateral adsorbate–adsorbate interactions. These interactions generate strong coverage dependence in adsorption energies and reaction barriers, often reshaping dominant pathways. They are notoriously difficult to map with DFT because of the combinatorial explosion of possible surface configurations. To address this challenge, Lym et al.93 introduced a lattice convolutional neural network capable of learning configuration- and coverage-dependent adsorption energies directly from DFT data, providing a fast surrogate that can be embedded into lattice kMC or microkinetic models. Building on the idea of correcting mean-field approximations, Tian and Rangarajan94 showed that neural networks can learn systematic, coverage-dependent corrections that reconcile mean-field microkinetics with lattice kMC in the fast-diffusion limit. More recently, Johnson et al.95 combined automated DFT workflows with machine-learning models to predict coverage-dependent rate constants for multi-step reaction networks, enabling microkinetic simulations that explicitly account for co-adsorbate effects. Another example is provided by Schwalbe-Koda et al.96, who developed a neural-network potential that enabled exhaustive sampling of millions of high-coverage surface configurations for CO and CO/CHOH co-adsorption, revealing how lateral interactions and site blocking reshape adsorption landscapes and reaction energetics. Sakai et al.97 used a similar strategy of sampling high-coverage configurations with a neural network potential to evaluate coverage effects in ethylene hydroformylation, coupling the high-coverage sampling and models with descriptor-based catalyst screening to evaluate the trends in coverage effects across different metals . Interestingly, Klumpers et al.98 used ML models to show that the dynamics of high-coverage adlayers are also important, using neural networks trained on DFT/MD data to extract lateral interaction energies in dynamic, finite-temperature adlayers, leading to strong agreement with experimental measurements. In a complementary strategy, Yokaichiya et al.99 directly embedded neural network models into an adaptive kMC simulation, implicitly capturing lateral interactions during a kMC simulation.

These studies demonstrate that ML approaches can now resolve coverage effects at scales and levels of configurational detail that are impractical with DFT alone, offering a viable path toward more realistic and predictive kinetic models.

3.3 Integration of AI/ML with multiscale and reactor models

The use of AI and ML models in reaction engineering and multiscale modeling is also increasing. Several studies focus on constructing ML surrogates for first-principles microkinetics, enabling reactor-scale simulations that retain mechanistic fidelity while dramatically reducing computational cost. For example, Biermann et al. 100 developed physics-enhanced neural networks that emulate a UBI-QEP microkinetic mechanism inside industrial packed-bed reactor calculations, while Döppel and Votsmeier 101built neural-network–based surrogates for rate-determining steps in first-principles Pt oxidation kinetics. Related work by Bracconi et al. and by Partopour et al. examines how ML models can rapidly approximate microkinetic rate maps or translate mechanistic reaction networks into efficient surrogate models for reactor design studies 102, 103. These approaches enable the integration of detailed kinetics with mass and heat transfer models that would be intractable using standard numerical methods.

Other efforts aim to use AI and ML methods to automate the entire multiscale workflow from DFT to reactor, such as the AMUSE framework of Sabadell-Rendón et al. 104, which constructs reaction networks and reactor simulations directly from ab initio energetics, and the work by Núñez and Vlachos105, which uses active learning to explore how nanoscale catalyst microstructure affects reactor-scale performance without any empirical parameter tuning.

Together, these works illustrate how ML can provide computational acceleration, automated model construction, and systematic exploration within fully mechanistic multiscale reactor frameworks.

3.4 Extracting kinetic parameters from measured reactor data

Once kinetic models based on complex reaction mechanisms have been built, AI and ML play an important role in confronting the results of the model with experimental data through optimization, creating more parsimonious models, or even replacing the bottom-up approach of building a kinetic model based on elementary steps by extracting mechanism or rate laws directly from experimental data. Pétremand et al. 106 posed the question of whether machine learning (ML)-based regressions can reliably describe kinetics without requiring detailed reaction mechanisms. A data set spanning various temperatures, pressures and space velocities for CO2 methanation on a Ni-based catalyst was employed to perform several ML-based regressions, the best of which were selected and assessed against two standard kinetic modeling approaches: power law and Langmuir–Hinshelwood–Hougen–Watson (LHHW). The ML-based models outperformed the power law and were comparable to the LHHW model, particularly when tested against data obtained from a nonisothermal reactor. Gusmão et al. 107 put forth the concept of kinetics-informed neural networks, where feed-forward artificial neural networks are used as basis functions to solve systems of DAEs, demonstrating that the simultaneous training of neural nets and kinetic model parameters leads to the solution of the inverse problem through the estimation of kinetic parameters from synthetic experimental data.

3.5 Using ML to extract kinetic equations

A related direction is the use of ML models to extract the form of the kinetic equations that underlie kinetic data. Brunton et al. 108 developed an approach termed the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) methodology, which sparked many derivatives 109 and similar approaches. For example, Prabhu and coworkers 110 developed an approach to learn interpretable dynamical models from data to handle inherent experimental noise by employing a new derivative-free technique that approximates the integral rather than the derivative and including domain information such as mass balance and chemistry information. Towards this same end, Van Dam and coworkers introduced Poly-ODENet 111 to address the challenge of discovering the rate laws (i.e., the “right-hand side” of a set of ODEs that describe kinetics of a reaction network following mass action) without knowing the reaction network, especially when the data are incomplete due to experimental limitations. Lejarza et al. 112, 24 take this a step further to address nonlinear systems in an integrated approach that obtains both rate laws and the associated parameters. Given a large set of candidate elementary reaction steps and experimental or simulated concentration data, they find the governing microkinetic model by simultaneously estimating the associated kinetic parameters (e.g., rate constants, activation energies, pre-exponential factors) and systematically eliminating insignificant/redundant elementary reaction steps. A common theme in many of the physics-informed machine learning for kinetic models is the use of known constraints. Although the details vary by model, most ML approaches for fitting kinetics exploit the known structure of the underlying differential equations by constraining the optimization to follow the law of mass action 111, 110. In addition, constraints related to site conservation, thermodynamic consistency, reaction stoichiometry and explicitly known reaction mechanisms have been used to restrict the model space to physically plausible models 113, 110, 107, 23.

3.6 Simultaneous model/experiment optimization of reaction conditions

Models play a critical role in the optimization of reaction conditions to realize optimal yields and selectivities, and ML is playing an increasingly significant role in the design loop for reactive processes. For example, Yang and coworkers 114 developed interpretable machine learning to accelerate the reverse design and optimization of methanation catalysts. To elucidate the intricate interplay among catalyst compositions, preparation conditions, reaction parameters, and catalytic performance, the authors developed different ML models, carried out an interpretable analysis to ascertain the most significant features, and then integrated the best performing model with an optimal multiobjective optimization algorithm to facilitate the reverse design of a low-temperature and highly active catalyst for CO2 methanation. Neumann and Palkovits 115 examined reinforcement learning approaches for the optimization of the partial oxidation of methane. Q-learning (QL) agents and deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) agents were trained to maximize hydrogen production by partial oxidation of methane, with the DDPG agent performing well and demonstrating how reinforcement learning can address a classic reactor optimization problem by adjusting temperature, pressure, flow velocity, and substrate composition. Zhang et al. 116 took on the challenge of applying an ensemble-learning approach to a classic chemical engineering operation, fluidized catalytic cracking (FCC), and showed a learning model can accurately predict the coke yield, noting that the model structure is simple and easy to construct, which provides performance advantages in FCC process modeling.

Machine learning has also shown value in studying processes that are less mature, including optimizing hydrogen production with Fe/g-C3N4 photocatalysts 117, and electrochemical reactors 118. Indeed, Luo et al.118 note that, because of the complexity of its reaction mechanism and the largely unknown electron transfer pathways, the development of a first-principles-based operational model of a CO2 electrocatalytic reactor is still in its infancy, and ML thus has an important role to play. Sheng et al. 119 demonstrate this as well, showing how an autonomous electrochemical platform that implements an adaptive, closed-loop workflow for mechanistic investigation of molecular electrochemistry can discern an electrochemical mechanism amid negative controls and outliers, adaptively design desired experimental conditions, and quantitatively extract kinetic information, from which mechanistic insights were gained, illustrating how ML can enable self-driving electrochemistry laboratories. In many of these cases, experiments themselves serve as validation of the models, either by evolving the model through active learning schemes, or by serving as a final validation of a model prediction.

Tools that enable researchers in the field to more easily adopt ML into their own workflows for kinetic analysis are being developed, as well as data benchmarks for chemical reactions 120, 121, 122. For example, Chemfit, developed by Jiscoot and coworkers, facilitates the evaluation of the experimental data quality and quantity requirements needed for the reliable discovery of the rates driving corresponding chemical models 123. While conversion of mechanisms in human-readable form into model files has long been a staple of automated network generation and associated kinetic model toolboxes, human/AI collaboration is taken one step further by leveraging LLM prompts to facilitate the process. For example, Li et al. introduce a workflow and open-source Python package, the Sanofi Kinetic AI (SKAI) tool 124, that simplifies kinetic modeling. SKAI incorporates a prompt-engineered large language model (LLM) that converts reaction descriptions into system equations.

3.7 Catalyst discovery and optimization

3.7.1 Accelerating high-throughput atomic-scale computational screening

Leveraging the modeling developments reviewed in Section 3.1, AI and ML are also accelerating the discovery of new catalytic molecules and materials by enabling high-throughput exploration of large compositional and structural spaces that would be prohibitively expensive to evaluate with DFT alone.

In heterogeneous catalysis, the Open Catalyst Project has established large-scale DFT datasets and benchmark tasks that support ML models capable of rapidly predicting adsorption energies for diverse surfaces, enabling orders-of-magnitude faster preliminary screening 66, 83. Complementary work by Li et al. 125 and Mao et al. 126 extends these ideas to bimetallic alloys and alloy nanoclusters, using neural-network or descriptor-based surrogates trained on DFT to target improved oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) or hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity across vast design spaces. Work by Pisal et al. expands on these ideas by using ML models to incorporate the influence of different sites and facets in the exploration of CO2-to-methanol catalyst compositions 127. Similar workflows have emerged for other classes of catalytic materials. For example, Zhang et al. employed multitask learning to predict multiple stability metrics across thousands of MOFs 128. On the molecular catalysis side, ML models trained on DFT-computed properties have been used to virtually screen redox-active transition-metal complexes, as demonstrated in work by Janet et al. 129. These efforts illustrate how ML-driven surrogates and learned descriptors can dramatically expand the chemical search space accessible to computation, enabling more efficient identification and optimization of promising catalyst candidates. In many of these cases, the final validation occurs by comparison with DFT simulations, rather than catalyst synthesis and testing. This is appropriate as a test of the ML models because it is not possible for them to exceed the quality of the data they were trained on, and there are many complexities that can cause real synthesized catalysts to have active sites different from those of the underlying atomistic models. These problems are typically tackled with additional types of AI/ML models such as response surface modeling and autonomous synthesis and testing platforms as described below.

Beyond high-throughput atomistic modeling, the approach of response-surface modeling has emerged as a powerful tool for experimental catalyst discovery and optimization, enabling systematic exploration of multidimensional formulation spaces that are difficult to navigate by intuition alone. In recent work, Uusitalo et al. used a response-surface model along with design-of-experiments to optimize bimetallic compositions for EMF hydrogenation, revealing nonlinear trade-offs between metal ratios and selectivity 130. In a related work, QSPR-based multitask learning models have been used to relate sorbent and catalyst formulation variables to multiple performance metrics 131. Response-surface models have also proven effective for identifying promising oxide mixtures for oxidative coupling of methane, as demonstrated in a formulation-focused study by Nishimura et al. 132, and for tuning the composition and preparation parameters of Cu-CHA catalysts through statistically guided parameter mapping 133. In addition, Alanazi et al. used response-surface models to optimize Ni–zeolite catalysts for methane conversion 134, and Zarei-Jelyani et al. employed response-surface models to tune metal ratios and promoter levels in Ni–Co–Ce/Al2O3 catalysts for steam-methane reforming 135. These studies illustrate how response-surface modeling can efficiently map catalyst formulation variables to activity and selectivity, acting as a form of experimental design that reduces the number of costly synthesis–testing cycles.

Generative AI techniques are opening a new frontier in catalyst discovery by enabling models to propose novel compositions and structures directly, rather than merely screening pre-existing candidates. Recent work on high-entropy alloy catalysts has shown that variational autoencoders (VAEs) can learn latent representations of multicomponent compositions and then generate previously unexplored alloy formulations with predicted catalytic promise 136, while condition-aware models such as CatDRX extend this idea by conditioning a VAE on reactants and products to generate homogeneous catalysts tailored to specific reaction environments 137.

Large-language-model (LLM) approaches offer a complementary generative strategy that takes advantage of natural language interfaces and pre-trained models. CatGPT demonstrates that transformer models can generate plausible catalyst formulations directly from textual prompts 138, and CataLM 139 and related LLM-based efforts 140 show how domain-specialized language models can suggest catalyst compositions, synthetic precursors, and design rationales grounded in chemical patterns learned from the training data or in-context prompts. More broadly, general frameworks such as MatterGen provide a route for sampling chemically valid crystal structures across large materials spaces, including catalytic materials, providing a route to establish new candidate materials 141. Finally, explainable generative models provide a degree of interpretability by linking latent-space directions to chemically meaningful formulation features, helping guide the rational modification of generated catalyst candidates 142. Together, these methods illustrate how generative AI is shifting catalyst discovery from screening toward creative, model-driven exploration of vast compositional and structural spaces.

Recent advances in autonomous experimentation are beginning to reshape catalyst discovery by merging high-throughput robotics with machine learning in fully closed-loop “smart lab” workflows. For example, Bennett et al.143 demonstrated the design of homogeneous catalysts for olefin hydroformylation using an autonomous “robotic chemist” that independently designed, synthesized, and optimized the ligands of a new Rh-based catalyst system while performing hundreds of experiments per day in a flow chemistry platform. Zhang et al.144 extended this concept to electrocatalysis by using a multimodal robotic platform with integrated rapid ink preparation, automated electrode fabrication, and active-learning–guided electrochemical testing to identify a top-performing multi-element catalyst for formate oxidation within only a few iterative loops. Bayesian-optimization–driven discovery has also been used for identification of new catalyst formulations for the reverse water–gas shift reaction 145, synthesis of higher alcohols from syngas 146, and the OER reaction in acid 147. Robotics-integrated platforms have further expanded electrocatalyst discovery by combining automated synthesis with ML-guided selection of experiments 148 and enabled closed-loop identification of chiral Rh-ligand homogeneous catalysts through autonomous enantioselectivity screening 149. These studies demonstrate how connecting AI and ML tools with automated experiments in fully or partially closed-loop systems can accelerate the discovery of new catalyst compositions.

Table 1 summarizes the findings of this section.

4 Thermodynamics, Transport and Fluid Mechanics

4.1 Transport Phenomena and Fluid Mechanics

Recent advances in AI/ML have broadened their applicability in transport phenomena and fluid mechanics, extending from data analysis to predictive modeling, design, and control across a wide range of flow systems. The studies discussed in this section share a common objective of using AI/ML to extract useful physical insights from complex experimental and computational data, improve the analysis of multiscale transport processes, and enhance predictions of nonlinear, multiphase, and three-dimensional unsteady flows. Although the applications span droplet-laden flows, bubble columns, boiling and phase-change systems, microfluidics, and environmental flows, they collectively illustrate the growing convergence of data-driven methods with classical transport theory. This progression has led to the development of hybrid and physics-based frameworks that combine machine learning with first-principles models to provide accurate, interpretable, and physically consistent predictions.

4.1.1 Analysis of complex multiphase phenomena

Machine learning has emerged as a transformative framework in fluid mechanics, enabling the analysis, prediction, and control of complex multiphase phenomena that are often difficult to capture using traditional theoretical or experimental methods 150, 151, 152. In multiphase systems, such as droplet-laden flows, processes including droplet deformation, fragmentation, coalescence, evaporation, and transport are inherently nonlinear, multiscale, and highly sensitive to small variations in operating conditions 153, 154. Conventional design and optimization strategies, relying on theoretical models, empirical correlations, or iterative experimentation, often struggle to efficiently resolve the associated spatiotemporal complexity 155, 156, 157. Recent progress in high-speed imaging, digital in-line holography, tomographic diagnostics, and high-fidelity simulations has enabled ML models to extract droplet characteristics and underlying flow physics with unprecedented accuracy, supporting both fundamental research and industrial applications 158, 159, 160, 161, 162. A notable recent development is the integration of deep learning architectures for droplet segmentation and flow-field reconstruction from computationally expensive simulations and complex experimental image datasets 163. Neural network architectures such as U-Net, R2-UNet, attention-based frameworks, and residual models can identify droplets directly from raw holographic or shadowgraphic data without conventional feature engineering 164, 165. Once trained, these models can rapidly process thousands of images, enabling time-resolved quantification of droplet size distributions (DSDs) across diverse fragmentation regimes, including bag breakup, sheet thinning, and ligament breakup. Compared with conventional thresholding or Hough-transform-based methods, ML-driven segmentation is particularly effective when droplets are overlapping, highly deformed, or form dense sprays 159. Beyond droplet detection, regression and classification models enable direct prediction of droplet size, velocity, and breakup mode from experimental or simulation data 166. Furthermore, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are now widely applied to characterize and model turbulent flows 167. These capabilities increasingly support inverse-design workflows, including atomizer optimization, prediction of raindrop formation in atmospheric flows 168, 169, and improvements in spray-based combustion systems 159, 160, 161.

AI/ML approaches have become indispensable tools for analyzing multiphase flows in industrial and environmental systems 168, 169, 170. In bubble column reactors, widely used in chemical, petrochemical, and biochemical industries, ML models have been employed to track bubble breakup, coalescence, residence time, and interfacial area, all of which critically influence mass transfer and reaction rates. Deep learning frameworks further enable reconstruction of bubble shapes from experimental or simulated data and prediction of gas holdup across a range of operating conditions 171, 170. These capabilities support accurate modeling of mixing, turbulence modulation, and transitions between flow regimes such as homogeneous, heterogeneous, and churn-turbulent states. Given the highly unsteady, three-dimensional nature of flow in bubble columns and the strong interphase coupling of heat and mass transfer, ML provides an efficient and scalable alternative to computationally expensive high-fidelity simulations 172.

Similar advances have been demonstrated in liquid–liquid extraction units, slurry reactors, fluidized beds, coastal sediment transport, and thermal phase-change systems, where ML facilitates real-time detection and quantification of dispersed phases 173. For example, in boiling heat transfer, segmentation networks accurately identify nucleation sites and departure diameters, while sequence-based models capture the temporal evolution of bubble dynamics. In spray cooling, AI models can monitor droplet size, velocity, and surface coverage to dynamically adjust nozzle flow rates or heating profiles for optimal thermal performance. In biomedical microfluidics, ML-controlled droplet generation enables adaptive modulation of breakup and merging processes for applications such as on-chip chemical reactions or single-cell encapsulation. In atmospheric and environmental applications, ML-enabled characterization of droplets and aerosols has improved modeling of rainfall formation, cloud microphysics, and pollutant transport. In particular, ML frameworks now predict droplet size distributions and inform strategies for cloud seeding, aerosol injection, and weather modification 168, 169. By integrating high-resolution measurements with physics-informed ML models, researchers are able to optimize droplet formation, growth, and coalescence under varying thermodynamic conditions, improving accuracy of rainfall predictions and supporting targeted environmental interventions.

These advances reduce reliance on large-scale field measurements while offering actionable guidance for engineering design and policy decisions. The convergence of ML with advanced sensing technologies, such as high-speed imaging, holography, and tomographic diagnostics, now enables real-time optimization, where fluid systems can adapt dynamically based on measured or predicted performance.

4.1.2 Hybrid modeling: Interfacing ML and physics-based models

One promising frontier is the synergy between ML and physics-based modeling 167, 174. Hybrid approaches, incorporating physical constraints into neural networks or using ML to accelerate Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) solvers, are reshaping droplet-laden flow simulations. PINNs, for example, solve governing equations like Navier–Stokes directly from data, reconstructing velocity and pressure fields from sparse measurements. For droplet dynamics, these models predict breakup thresholds, surface instabilities, and interfacial forces without requiring full numerical simulations. Reinforcement learning (RL) is also being explored for multiphase system control, such as optimizing atomization processes, modulating bubble distributions in reactors, and designing active feedback in spray cooling. With advances in sensor networks and high-speed imaging, real-time ML-based control of multiphase flows is becoming increasingly feasible. In industrial practice, AI/ML-driven design and optimization demonstrate clear advantages across chemical, petrochemical, and process engineering applications. For example, in bubble column reactors, models trained on experimental or CFD data predict the effects of operational changes on bubble breakup, coalescence, residence time, and interfacial area, enabling optimization of reactor geometry, sparger design, and flow conditions without extensive experimental campaigns 171, 170, 172. In heat-transfer systems, ML models optimize boiling bubble dynamics or fine-tune droplet spray cooling patterns for enhanced thermal performance. In liquid–liquid extraction units, ML guides impeller and packing design and flow rates to improve separation efficiency by predicting droplet dispersion and coalescence under varying operational conditions 173.

Looking ahead, the integration of AI/ML into fluid mechanics represents a paradigm shift in system design and optimization. While traditional analytical, empirical, and computational approaches remain foundational, AI/ML complements them by enabling rapid, high-dimensional optimization, real-time feedback control, and exploration of otherwise intractable design spaces. The combination of physics-informed modeling, deep learning-based data extraction, and reinforcement learning-driven control is creating fluid systems that are self-optimizing, adaptive, and highly efficient.

Overall, AI and ML are evolving from tools for analysis or simulation to central components of modern fluid system design. By integrating high-fidelity measurement, predictive modelling, and optimization within a unified framework, these approaches reduce development cycles, lower costs, enhance operational efficiency, and enable next-generation devices across industrial, environmental, and biomedical applications. From high-performance chemical reactors to advanced droplet-based microfluidics and large-scale atmospheric interventions, AI/ML-driven design is transforming how fluid systems are conceived, optimized, and controlled, ushering in a new era where intelligent, data-driven strategies are indispensable to fluid mechanics research and engineering 159, 170, 174.

The models discussed in this section directly address several of the key challenges outlined in the Introduction. In terms of predictive accuracy, ML-enabled frameworks leverage high-fidelity simulation and experimental data to capture complex, nonlinear multiphase dynamics that are difficult to resolve using conventional models. Challenges associated with limited or noisy data are mitigated through hybrid and physics-informed approaches, which incorporate governing equations and known physical constraints to regularize learning and improve robustness. Importantly, many of these models explicitly enforce material and energy conservation by embedding conservation laws (e.g., mass, momentum, and energy balances) into the model architecture or loss functions, as in physics-informed neural networks and hybrid CFD–ML frameworks. This ensures physically consistent predictions, even in regimes with sparse data or during extrapolation. Furthermore, interpretability is enhanced by integrating ML components within established transport equations, enabling model predictions to be analyzed in the context of known fluid-mechanical principles. Finally, these approaches improve extrapolation capability and model reliability by restricting predictions to physically admissible solution spaces, thereby aligning data-driven learning with first-principles understanding.

4.2 Thermodynamics

4.2.1 Thermodynamic and transport property prediction

Over the past decade, the number of publications explicitly incorporating ML for thermodynamic property prediction has grown remarkably, with a large fraction relying on regression algorithms and artificial neural networks (ANNs) to represent thermodynamic behavior, especially for systems where traditional physical models are difficult to develop or for emerging families of compounds that can be tuned and easily expanded, such as ionic liquids or deep eutectic solvents 175. While many contributions have reported successful results for specific properties, a central limitation of supervised learning methods is the need for large and well-labeled datasets, whereas thermophysical property data are often incomplete or unevenly reported. Consequently, many ANN-based studies have been hindered by data scarcity, inconsistency, and limited coverage of chemical space 176.

Additionally, ML has also been increasingly used to estimate transport properties such as viscosity177, 178, thermal conductivity179, 178, ionic conductivity180, and diffusion coefficients181—properties that lie beyond the predictive scope of most equations of state and typically rely on semi-empirical correlations. Data-driven models can offer competitive or superior predictive performance for these properties by leveraging molecular descriptors, state variables, and nonlinear regression algorithms. This body of work has also highlighted the importance of model interpretability and feature relevance when applying ML to transport phenomena, emphasizing both the opportunities and methodological challenges associated with replacing or complementing traditional correlations 182, 183.

Another key trend in recent years is the incorporation of thermodynamic constraints directly into the ML architecture or loss function. These “thermodynamics-informed” ML approaches embed identities such as the Gibbs–Helmholtz or Clausius–Clapeyron relations, ensuring internal consistency and improving extrapolation performance in low-data regimes184. Integrating molecular information with explicit thermodynamic constraints improves robustness, reduces unphysical predictions, and relates ML outputs to established physical behavior 185. This effort aligns with the broader shift toward ML models that respect conservation laws, convexity of free energies, stability of phases, and other fundamental requirements of thermodynamics, as discussed in Section 4.1.2.

As also emphasized in Section 3.1, at the microscopic level, ML has transformed atomistic simulations, which are central to thermodynamic property prediction. State-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials can now reproduce ab initio accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, making it feasible to evaluate thermodynamic properties of large systems over long timescales 186. Simultaneously, ML within statistical mechanics has enabled data-driven mappings between microscopic configurations and macroscopic thermodynamic functions, accelerating the estimation of free energies, phase behavior, and phase diagrams, even expanding exploration of compositional and thermodynamic state spaces 187.

Parallelling recent trends in catalyst design (Section 3.7.1), beyond forward prediction, ML is increasingly used for inverse problems: given target thermodynamic behavior, infer molecular architecture, mixture composition, or operating conditions. Several recent efforts combine chemical representations with SAFT-based approaches to map SMILES strings and molecular fingerprints 188, 189, or σ\sigma-profiles 190 to equation of state (EoS) parameters, enabling rapid screening of virtual molecular libraries for desired phase behavior or critical properties.

A complementary line of work replaces or augments the EoS with neural networks constrained by thermodynamics. Neural-network surrogate models can be trained to represent free energies, from which all thermodynamic quantities are derived, thereby ensuring consistency by construction 191. Similar models explicitly embed phase transitions and stability criteria within the network architecture and loss function 192. Collectively, these methods mark a shift from purely black-box regressors toward hybrid frameworks in which ML augments, rather than replaces, thermodynamic theory.

Despite impressive progress, multiple challenges remain. Data scarcity, inconsistency, and heterogeneity across sources (different laboratories, measurement standards, or purity levels) limit the reliability of purely data-driven models. Ensuring thermodynamic consistency, respecting Maxwell relations, convexity of free energies, and positivity of entropy production remains difficult for generic ML architectures, motivating continued development of physics-informed designs. Extrapolation beyond the training domain, crucial for process synthesis and safety, remains a persistent weakness. Furthermore, integrating ML-based thermodynamic modules into process modeling/design software requires robust uncertainty quantification, transparent validation, and long-term maintainability.

Overall, the field is evolving from simple property regression toward hybrid frameworks in which ML augments, rather than replaces, thermodynamic modeling. The combination of high-fidelity simulation data, curated experimental databases, and physics-informed ML architectures promises fast, accurate, and generalizable thermodynamic models for emerging fluids and applications. Table 2 summarizes the findings of this section.

5 Separations

ML has had significant impacts on separation processes across length scales, from materials to process design and optimization.

5.1 Gas-Liquid Contact Operations

Distillation remains the key technology for separating liquid mixtures in industry 193. The fundamentals principles are generally well understood, but applications challenges remain, particularly in the case of separating complex and/or multi-component streams. These include, e.g., mixtures encountered in refining, that are characterized using empirical fractions rather than at the molecular level 194, 195, and mixtures with impurities 196.

At the design level, 197 demonstrated the potential of generative AI for distillation column design. Leveraging variational autoencoders, it was shown that generative AI can generate novel configurations, ensure purity constraints, and boost efficiency, while outperforming discriminative AI in process intensification innovation. 198 demonstrated the use of ML for optimizing the energy use in distillation, while 199 undertook a similar effort at the process level.

200 discuss the use of interpretable ML for predicting the performance of high-gravity NOx oxidation/absorption, a complex intensified operation. In a similar vein, 201 used ML tools to predict hydrodynamic properties in a rotating disc contactor.

5.2 Separation Materials

5.2.1 Adsorbents

Among the emerging classes of adsorbents, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have been by far the most widely studied due to their high surface areas and tunable adsorption properties 202, 203, 204. Their reticular structure and thus modular nature also make them an excellent candidate for ML-based study. One of the most significant enabling studies in this field was the release of the Computation-Ready Experimental (CoRE) MOF database by Snurr and colleagues.205 This database and subsequent updates and extensions have provided researchers with tens of thousands of structural files of MOFs that have been experimentally synthesized and characterized in wet labs across the world.206 This database has provided a fertile ground for using ML to explore the gas separation properties of MOFs for applications such as noble gas separation,207 paraffin/olefin separation,208, 209 and CO2 capture.210, 211, 212 These workflows have even been integrated with Ideal Adsorbed Solution Theory calculations to predict binary gas adsorption behavior.213

Several studies have leveraged ML to navigate this expanded MOF space consisting of millions of adsorbent candidates.202, 214, 215 Of note, the use of ML has now moved far beyond simple screening. For example, one of the most exciting applications is the use of ML models to generate entirely new MOFs for targeted applications.216 Fu et al. developed MOFDiff, which leveraged a diffusion model architecture to create coarse-grained MOF representations that were then decoded to full atomistic representation and optimized for CO2 capture.217 In another study, Aspuru-Guzik and co-workers used a variational autoencoder architecture to generate a customized text-based representation that was then used to build all new MOFs for CO2 separations, resulting in several candidates competitive with the state of the art.218 Generative MOF design is now incorporated into large language model (LLM) studies through the development of ChatMOF by Kang and Kim. They leveraged GPT-4 to create an agentic pipeline for searching, predicting, and generating new MOFs targeted at CO2 capture.219 Clearly, ML has opened a world of exciting possibilities to translate materials discovery with pressing gas separations challenges that are critical to chemical engineering.

5.2.2 Membranes

With the rapid development of membrane separation technologies based on emerging functional materials — including two-dimensional materials 220, 221, 222 (e.g., graphene, graphene oxide and MXene), framework materials (e.g., metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) 223 and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) 224), and advanced porous polymers 225 — it has become possible to achieve highly selective separation of small ions and molecules for applications ranging from water desalination to resource recovery and gas purification. This progress stems from the rational engineering of membrane structures, surface chemistries, and pore architectures to precisely regulate transport pathways. For example, in water treatment processes, multiscale separations occur through a combination of microfiltration, ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, and reverse osmosis, requiring fine control of molecular sieving and electrostatic exclusion mechanisms 226. Similarly, lithium extraction from brines demands sub-nanometer discrimination between Li+ and Mg2+ ions 227, 228, while gas separation membranes often rely on subtle differences in molecular diffusivity and adsorption enthalpy to achieve efficient CO2/N2 or H2/CO2 separation 223, 229. In this context, the integration of AI into separation processes is opening new avenues for understanding and optimizing selective transport phenomena, bridging macroscopic flow behavior with angstrom-scale interfacial interactions within confined pores.

ML has been extensively used in the design and development of new materials for polymeric membranes. In particular, Ramprasad and colleagues have contributed to the development of the Polymer Genome database. At release, Polymer Genome uses a fingerprinting scheme to featurize polymers for surrogate models and predict a variety of useful physical properties such as glass transition temperature, dielectric constant, etc.230 It has since undergone several updates to include prediction of gas permeability through membranes formed from polymers.231 Ramprasad and colleagues have also made further contributions to the field by developing multi-task ML models that can predict diffusion coefficients, solubility coefficients, and permeabilities for both gases232 and complex organic solvent separations,233 highlighting both the diversity of potential use cases of polymer membranes in chemical separations and the utility of ML in navigating the structure–performance space in a rational and physically insightful way.

ML has also been applied to other topics within membrane science beyond gas separation performance with pure polymers. For example, mixed-matrix membranes (MMMs), in which secondary materials are dispersed in polymers to improve overall transport properties, are widely studied. ML has been used for in silico screening to find the optimum dispersed/continuous phase combinations for industrially relevant separations such as CO2/CH4234 and H2/CH4.235 Another interesting application is using ML to understand the most relevant factors to ion transport through nanoporous membranes, which has implications in both water treatment and metal recovery.236 A recurring trend in many of these studies is the use of experimental data and its homogenization with selected data derived from molecular simulations, which stands in contrast to most ML studies of MOF adsorbents that use entirely simulated datasets from molecular dynamics or Grand Canonical Monte Carlo methods. This observation supports that quality ML models can be developed with thoughtful design, even on comparably smaller datasets, which highlights the benefit of using data from disparate sources to build more robust models.

5.3 Module and Process Modeling

In addition to the vast body of work on using ML to improve the molecular design of separations materials, it has also been used by several researchers to improve the design of process units using these materials. Adsorption processes are a common target due to their well-established operating principles and well-defined governing equations.

Pai et al. developed the machine-assisted adsorption process learning and emulation (MAPLE) framework, built on a dense feedforward network with Bayesian regularization, to optimize a vacuum swing adsorption (VSA) cycle for CO2/N2 separation from single-component isotherms.237 They later built on this model by incorporating governing differential transport equations and expanding the range of application to include chromatography to create a physics-based artificial neural network framework for adsorption and chromatography emulation (PANACHE). PANACHE achieved 100 ×\times improvement in computation time compared to traditional solvers while maintaining a high degree of fidelity to the underlying physics.238

5.3.1 Multiscale Modeling and Design

Thermodynamics defines the energy landscape governing selective transport across membranes, linking driving forces such as osmotic pressure, chemical potential gradients, and interfacial free energies with separation efficiency.

Conventional, physics-based modeling platforms that are frequently used in this field, such as MATLAB and COMSOL rely on deterministic formulations (e.g., Poisson–Nernst–Planck equations 239, 240) to describe ion diffusion, advection, and permeation through selective media.

However, these approaches often struggle to capture the nonlinear couplings among pore structure, surface chemistry, and fluid behavior. In subnanofluidic and ion-selective systems, traditional thermodynamic models also fail to account for multicomponent interactions, hydration-shell restructuring, and specific surface–solute interactions that govern selectivity. Although molecular dynamics simulations can quantify energy barriers, binding energies, and dehydration effects for ions traversing subnanometer channels 241, 242, 243, they remain limited by computational cost and system size.

As in the case of kinetics and thermodynamics modeling (Sections 3.7.1 and 4.1.2, AI provides a powerful complementary approach by learning membrane-relevant thermodynamic relationships directly from experimental and simulation datasets while embedding physical constraints 244, 245, 246, 247, 248. Machine learning models can accurately predict key thermodynamic parameters—including osmotic pressures, activity coefficients, and hydration enthalpies—across wide ionic-strength and mixed-electrolyte ranges, frequently outperforming empirical correlations 249, 250, 251, 252.

Hybrid thermodynamic–AI frameworks further enable dynamic coupling of energetic terms (chemical potential differences, interfacial free-energy barriers, entropy changes) with transport kinetics, yielding more predictive descriptions of membrane processes and allowing real-time optimization under variable operating conditions. By integrating high-dimensional data from MD, transport measurements, and process operation with fundamental physical laws, AI can uncover hidden transport mechanisms, guide membrane design, and enhance predictive performance across applications ranging from high-salinity desalination to mixed-gas separations.

In the realm of adsorption, Grimm and Gazzani relied on multiscale modeling for selecting optimal sorbents for dilute CO2 capture via a vacuum–temperature swing adsorption process. Their model was highly computation-efficient because they reduced their modeling framework to a series of simple algebraic equations rather than more complex partial differential equations and were able to rapidly screen over 2,500 potential adsorbents and validate their viability for a full-scale adsorption process.253 In another integrated study, Ji and co-workers developed a random forest ML model to predict the ethane/ethylene adsorption behavior of hundreds of thousands of MOFs and then used this information with a VSA model to identify several candidate MOFs with high process-level performance.254 From these examples, it is clear that ML will be a critical tool to the future improvement of all aspects of separation processes.

5.3.2 System Operations

Beyond predictive modeling, AI is also revolutionizing how fluid transport is controlled and engineered in separation systems. Reinforcement learning and advanced optimization algorithms can autonomously tune operating parameters such as pressure gradients, concentration distributions, and temperature fields to maximize selectivity and permeation flux while minimizing energy consumption. For example, in water desalination, AI-based control strategies can adaptively adjust operating conditions to minimize fouling and energy use 244, whereas in lithium extraction, AI may optimize electro-driven transport pathways to enhance selectivity between competing ions 227, 228. Generative models and inverse design strategies further accelerate the discovery of novel membrane materials and channel architectures with targeted transport properties. Importantly, AI can identify emergent behaviors at complex fluid–solid interfaces — including cooperative ion transport, nanoscale flow instabilities, and dynamic fouling phenomena — that are often inaccessible to conventional analytical or numerical methods. This convergence of AI and transport science is poised to transform membrane separation engineering from an empirical discipline into an intelligent, adaptive, and predictive technology platform.

Table 3 summarizes existing progress and future opportunities in the Separations area.

6 Materials and Interfaces, and Applied Chemistry

The discovery and optimization of functional materials has long constrained the pace of technological advancement. Traditional experimental campaigns, from a pessimistic view reliant on serendipity and incremental refinement, struggle to navigate the combinatorial vastness of chemical composition space. As previewed in Sections 3.7.1 and 5.2, ML architectures now offer a fundamentally different paradigm. Rather than exhaustive enumeration, these computational frameworks learn underlying structure-property relationships from existing data, enabling rapid screening of candidate materials that would require decades of laboratory effort through conventional approaches 255. This transformation extends beyond acceleration and reshapes how researchers can conceptualize the discovery process itself.

A comprehensive review of crystalline materials prediction highlights how ML models now routinely estimate solubility, melting point, adsorption capacity, band gap, and electrochemical properties with accuracy rivaling conventional density functional theory (DFT), while dramatically reducing computational cost 256. Similarly, ensemble ML strategies combining XGBoost, SVM, ridge regression, and random forest models have been successfully applied to predict dielectric strength, dielectric constant, and electron affinity of organic compounds, demonstrating the maturity of supervised AI in high-dimensional chemical feature spaces 257. These studies collectively establish that data-driven models can capture complex nonlinear structure-property relationships across diverse chemical domains.

Graph neural networks (GNNs), which are notable tools for representing molecular and crystalline systems, have further advanced this capability by enabling descriptor-free learning directly from molecular graphs and periodic crystal structures. Instead of relying on predefined handcrafted features, GNN architectures encode atomic environments as nodes within connected graphs, capturing local coordination chemistry and long-range structural motifs simultaneously 258. The approach is flexible. Small organic molecules, extended inorganic frameworks, and amorphous interfaces can all be represented within unified computational schemas. This, in turn, facilitates learning across disparate chemical domains. 259 demonstrated that such graph-based representations achieve near-density functional theory (DFT) accuracy for a range of property predictions, including formation energies, band gaps, and elastic moduli, while reducing computational costs by several orders of magnitude. As discussed in recent reviews of crystalline property prediction, graph-based models excel in representing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), energetic materials, and electrochemical systems across multiple scales 256.
