These architectures allow unified treatment of small molecules, extended frameworks, and particle-scale crystalline products, facilitating cross-domain transferability and improved generalization. Similar developments have been made in graph kernels, which can be used to build probabilistic models over molecules as graphs 260, 261.

Importantly, AI-driven materials discovery has expanded beyond forward prediction toward generative and inverse design. Generative models such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) and conditional VAEs (CVAE) have been employed to explore vast chemical design spaces by learning continuous latent representations of molecular structures. For example, a CVAE framework was used to design supported ionic liquid membranes (SILMs) for CO2 capture, generating candidate membranes from limited experimental data and achieving strong agreement between predicted and experimentally measured CO2 absorption capacities 262. In parallel, VAE models combined with graph neural network property predictors and reinforcement learning have enabled inverse molecular design of surfactants with targeted critical micelle concentration values, demonstrating controlled navigation of chemical latent space toward predefined property thresholds 263. These approaches mark a conceptual shift from predicting properties of known materials to proposing entirely new materials optimized for desired performance.

As emphasized in Section 3.7.1, that covered catalyst discovery, the broader frontier of materials informatics now lies in the integration of AI with laboratory automation. Recent advances demonstrate that the coupling of machine learning algorithms, including Transformers and large language models (LLMs), with high-throughput experimentation platforms has enabled autonomous optimization of MOF synthesis conditions 264. The emergence of self-driving laboratories (SDLs), in which AI models iteratively propose experimental conditions, automated platforms execute synthesis and characterization, and newly acquired data refine the predictive model, represents a closed-loop paradigm for materials discovery. This convergence of predictive modeling, generative design, and robotic experimentation transitions AI from a passive analytical tool to an active driver of experimental decision-making.

Finally, an important distinguishing feature of many current-generation materials informatics models, relative to earlier quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) efforts, is the explicit encoding of physical constraints directly into the model architecture. E(3)-equivariant architectures 265 build on group theory to ensure that learned representations transform correctly under rotations and translations. This mathematical system yields improvements in data efficiency, notably for models requiring thousands of training examples, which, under conventional architectures, can achieve comparable performance with hundreds when symmetry constraints are encoded. The implications for novel chemistries where data is scarce are significant.

6.1 Benchmark Datasets and Computational Infrastructure

Standardized evaluation protocols underpin reproducibility in computational disciplines, and materials informatics is no exception. The Matbench initiative established systematic benchmarks for formation energy prediction, band gap estimation, and elastic modulus calculation, enabling comparisons across algorithmic approaches 266. These datasets, curated from the Materials Project repository, encompass tens of thousands of compounds with DFT-computed properties, providing sufficient statistical power to distinguish genuine methodological advances from artifacts of specific train-test splits.

The Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) dataset, designed to address the challenges of heterogeneous catalysis, represents perhaps the most ambitious community effort in this domain. It is comprised of over 1.2 million DFT relaxations across diverse surface-adsorbate configurations 66. Subsequent extensions through OC22 incorporated oxide electrocatalysts, addressing limitations of the initial release while expanding coverage to technologically critical reaction systems 83. Together, these resources contribute to the development of ML models capable of predicting adsorption energies with mean absolute errors approaching 0.2 eV. This is sufficient for preliminary catalyst screening, though still inadequate for quantitative kinetic modeling.

For large-scale materials screening, cloud high-performance computing (HPC) provides accessibility to the necessary computational resources. 267 demonstrated end-to-end workflows integrating ML geometric optimization with DFT validation, processing over 32 million candidate structures to identify 18 promising solid electrolytes for battery applications. The computational architecture leveraged Azure Quantum Elements, with ML inference requiring approximately 46 seconds per structure-relaxation step across 38,000 node-hours in total. Such throughput was unimaginable a decade ago. It reflects both algorithmic advances in ML potential accuracy and infrastructural investments in distributed computing platforms.

6.2 Universal Machine Learning Potentials

Continuing the discussion on MLIPs in Section 3.1.1, we note that the development of interatomic potentials applicable across the entire periodic table represents a key moment for computational materials science. Classical force fields, parameterized for specific element combinations, cannot capture the diversity of bonding environments encountered when exploring novel compositions. Universal ML potentials aim to circumvent this limitation by leveraging learned representations that generalize across the chemical space 268. M3GNet, trained on Materials Project relaxation trajectories, has been shown to achieve formation energy errors below 30 meV/atom while predicting forces with accuracy sufficient for geometry optimization. CHGNet extends this framework by incorporating explicit charge representations, thereby improving performance for ionic systems where electrostatic interactions dominate 269.

The GNoME project scaled these approaches dramatically. 270 reported the discovery of 2.2 million stable crystal structures through iterative cycles of ML prediction and DFT validation, expanding the known stable materials database by an order of magnitude. The significance extends beyond the sheer numbers. Many predicted structures occupy previously unexplored regions of composition space, suggesting that conventional intuition about chemical stability may be systematically incomplete. Through experimentation, novel phases have been validated, demonstrating that computational predictions can translate into laboratory reality with this approach.

For state-of-the-art accuracy with limited training data, equivariance constraints are essential. Tensor field networks introduced explicit rotational and translational symmetries via spherical harmonic expansions 271, an approach further refined in the NequIP and Allegro architectures 265. These models achieve chemical accuracy on molecular dynamics benchmarks while maintaining computational efficiency compatible with nanosecond-scale simulations. The practical consequence is a step-change as researchers can now explore conformational landscapes and reaction pathways that previously required (prohibitively) expensive ab initio molecular dynamics.

6.3 Autonomous Discovery Platforms

Laboratory automation is moving from convenient sample handling to scientific autonomy. Self-driving laboratories integrate robotic synthesis, automated characterization, and ML-guided decision-making within closed-loop optimization frameworks. 272 demonstrated this paradigm for thin-film photovoltaic materials, achieving relatively quick identification of optimal compositions through iterative Bayesian optimization. Their platform executed synthesis-characterization cycles faster than human researchers could analyze individual results. This not only changes the speed of discovery but also the economics of experimental exploration.

Building on the discussion in Section 3.7.1, we note here the work of 273, who extended automation to mobile robotic systems capable of operating continuously without human intervention. Over an eight-day campaign, their robotic chemist explored the photocatalyst formulation space, conducting more than 688 experiments to identify compositions with enhanced hydrogen-evolution activity. The system exhibited adaptive behavior, modifying sampling strategies based on accumulated evidence rather than following predetermined experimental plans. This adaptability is important when navigating high-dimensional parameter spaces where optimal regions cannot be anticipated from prior knowledge.

Perhaps the most ambitious integration of computational prediction with autonomous synthesis to date is the A-Lab platform. 274. While the success rates are subject to discussion275, real materials were synthesized and characterized without human hands touching the equipment, as demonstrated by algorithmic predictions.

Examples have emerged in which industrial adoption follows academic demonstrations. Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) implemented automated sintering workstations capable of validating 200 battery material formulations daily. This reduced development cycles by eight months compared to traditional workflows. Tesla's 4680 battery development leveraged automated testing systems that compressed charge-discharge characterization from 70 hours to 6 hours per sample 276. These implementations have demonstrated that autonomous laboratory concepts can be scaled to manufacturing-relevant levels. However, the diversity of synthesis routes and characterization techniques required across different material classes remains a limitation for wide-reaching adoption.

6.4 Implementation and Deployment Barriers

Even impressive benchmark metrics can obscure fundamental limitations for practical utility. Most ML potentials demonstrate accuracy on thermodynamic properties under equilibrium conditions. However, practical industrial applications frequently involve non-equilibrium phenomena: catalysts undergoing deactivation, membranes experiencing fouling, coatings degrading under environmental stress. Integrating time-dependent behavior into architectures designed for static property prediction remains an open challenge. Physics-informed approaches that encode kinetic pathways and mass-transfer limitations offer promising directions, although systematic validation across industrially relevant scenarios remains lacking 277.

Another issue is out-of-distribution generalization. 278 systematically probed ML model performance on materials differing structurally from training distributions, finding substantial accuracy degradation for compositions involving underrepresented elements or unusual coordination environments. These insights carry significant implications for discovery workflows that explicitly target novel chemistry. If models perform well only on materials resembling those already known, the promised exploration of uncharted chemical space may prove more limited than current projections suggest.

Data heterogeneity and deficiencies in standardization compound technical challenges. FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles enjoy rhetorical endorsement throughout the materials community, but practical implementation varies across repositories 279. Metadata inconsistencies, missing uncertainty quantifications, and incompatible file formats prevent cross-dataset training, which would otherwise maximize data utility. Initiatives such as NOMAD Laboratory279 aim to address these limitations, though achieving community-wide harmonization requires sustained coordination that often conflicts with immediate research priorities.

Closely related to, but distinct from, data standardization is the question of computational reproducibility, which we identify in the Introduction as a precondition for verifiable and comparable AI/ML research. In materials informatics specifically, benchmark leaderboards and reported accuracies are difficult to interpret when the training/test splits, featurization pipelines, hyperparameter search, and trained model checkpoints behind a given number are not released alongside it. Two papers reporting similar headline accuracy on, e.g., a MOF property-prediction task may not be comparable at all if one used a random split and the other a scaffold-based split, or if undisclosed hyperparameter tuning budgets differed substantially. Requiring code, data splits, trained weights, and versions of software/environments as a condition of publication, as is increasingly the norm in adjacent computational chemistry venues, would materially reduce the effort currently spent reimplementing published materials-discovery workflows from incomplete descriptions.

6.5 Transfer-Based MOF models

Several converging developments suggest imminent transformation in how materials are conceived, synthesized, and deployed. Foundation models trained on multimodal data, encompassing crystallographic structures, spectroscopic signatures, process parameters, and scientific literature, promise unprecedented integration of experimental and computational knowledge streams 280. Whether such models achieve genuine scientific reasoning or merely sophisticated pattern matching remains contested, but their potential to accelerate literature synthesis and hypothesis generation is substantial.

The introduction of Transformer models, originally developed for natural language processing, has emerged as a breakthrough across diverse scientific domains 281. Their self-attention mechanism enables the natural capture of both local and long-range atomic interactions that govern key properties of porous materials, particularly MOFs (see Section 5.2). These properties include porosity, gas adsorption, and structural stability. This allows Transformers to overcome the limited receptive field and message-passing constraints inherent to GNNs. They support highly parallel training, scale efficiently to large-scale MOF datasets, and facilitate powerful self-supervised pre-training and transfer learning, thereby reducing reliance on labeled data. Moreover, they avoid rigid graph priors and flexibly adapt to diverse MOF topologies and crystal structures while providing improved interpretability through attention weights. Collectively, these advantages significantly enhance performance in property prediction, inverse design, and multi-task modeling for MOF systems. Recent advances in Transformers have shifted MOF discovery from property-specific regression models to generalized, foundation-model approaches. A key capability driving this shift is the decoupling of feature extraction from explicit 3D atomic coordinates. For instance, structure-agnostic models leveraging text-based representations (e.g., MOFormer) can extract robust topological and elemental features directly from MOFid strings, circumventing the computational bottleneck of 3D structure generation 214. Furthermore, the development of multi-modal frameworks (e.g., MOFTransformer) enables the simultaneous integration of localized atom-based graphs and global energy-grid embeddings. This dual-modal approach facilitates universal transfer learning across thermodynamic, kinetic, and electronic properties 215. Another transformative capability is the incorporation of explicit operating conditions (e.g., temperature, pressure, gas type) directly into the model architecture (e.g., Uni-MOF) 282. This integration allows for robust cross-system generalization, such as extrapolating high-pressure adsorption behaviors strictly from low-pressure simulation data, which significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with traditional high-pressure screening.

While attention mechanisms offer interpretability that aligns well with chemical intuition by linking local chemistry to electronic properties and grid embeddings to diffusion, critical bottlenecks remain. Current models are heavily reliant on large-scale hypothetical databases (e.g., hMOF) that lack synthesis feasibility annotations. Consequently, algorithms frequently identify “high-performance” hypothetical candidates that are synthetically inaccessible. Additionally, while current models predict pure-component uptakes with high accuracy, their performance degrades when addressing dynamic, multicomponent industrial conditions. For example, explicitly predicting whether competitive gas separation is fundamentally driven by thermodynamic factors (especially when kinetic adsorption rates are identical) remains a complex challenge that current data-driven models struggle to capture without explicit physical constraints.

Moving forward, chemical engineers must ensure that the screening, design, and synthesis of novel materials are explicitly directed toward practical industrial deployment. At present, available datasets and machine learning models predominantly focus on predicting equilibrium gas adsorption and separation performance based on adsorption isotherms. While these thermodynamic metrics are necessary, translating a newly discovered material into a viable industrial technology requires a comprehensive evaluation of dynamic factors. Specifically, both adsorption and desorption kinetics must be integrated alongside thermodynamic data to determine the final engineering process configuration. Therefore, a critical priority is the development of end-to-end predictive models capable of bridging the gap between fundamental material properties and optimal industrial process conditions. Achieving this direct translation from material discovery to process engineering remains a significant challenge, marking a long but essential path ahead for the field. Furthermore, standardizing benchmarking protocols is essential to address prevalent issues of poor data hygiene and overfitting in materials discovery. Currently, many machine learning evaluations rely on random data splits, which often lead to data leakage due to the high structural similarity between training and test sets. To ensure fair model evaluation, researchers must adopt strict, out-of-distribution data splitting strategies, such as topology-based or scaffold-based splits, to rigorously test true generalization capabilities. Additionally, proposed deep learning architectures must be critically evaluated against well-tuned traditional baselines, rather than weak comparators, to justify their increased computational cost. Incorporating rigorous statistical tests to verify the practical significance of performance improvements is also necessary. Adopting these strict comparison protocols will ensure that models learn underlying chemical principles rather than simply memorizing dataset biases.

6.6 Future Trajectories and Research Imperatives

Sustainability considerations must permeate materials discovery frameworks more thoroughly than current practice allows. Most optimization objectives target performance metrics, with environmental impact relegated to post-hoc assessment. Embedding lifecycle analysis directly into generative design algorithms would enable discovery of materials balancing functional requirements with carbon footprint, supply chain resilience, and end-of-life recyclability. 283, 284 demonstrated that systematic consideration of these factors can identify materials with superior sustainability profiles among otherwise equivalent candidates, suggesting a significant opportunity for improvement.

The rise of LLMs as interfaces between researchers and analytical systems may prove as consequential as the underlying algorithmic advances. Natural language interaction lowers adoption barriers, enabling operators and engineers without specialized programming expertise to query complex databases, explore what-if scenarios, and interpret ML predictions within familiar conversational frameworks. Commercial offerings from multiple vendors are entering this space, though validation of LLM-generated scientific claims requires significant attention to hallucination risks, citation verification and interpretation, and overall reliability. LLMs have demonstrated substantial potential in reticular chemistry, encompassing literature mining, material design, and synthesis automation 285. Notably, this potential extends to the targeted design and synthesis of materials tailored to specific performance requirements, enabling data-driven optimization of structure-property relationships. 286 reported an innovative AI-driven workflow for catalyst optimization, with ammonia synthesis catalyst development as a case study, by integrating ChatGPT-based large LLMs with Bayesian optimization and an active learning loop 286. Specifically, LLMs were employed to mine scientific literature and construct a comprehensive chemical space for catalyst synthesis, while Bayesian optimization enabled iterative parametric optimization within this space. This integrated approach successfully predicted the optimal activation parameters for the Co3Mo3N ammonia synthesis catalyst, thereby significantly streamlining the catalyst development process and enhancing its overall efficiency.

It is critical to establish quantitative relationships between material properties and process performance metrics, including selectivity, conversion, energy consumption, and fouling rates to realize the full benefits of ML and AI materials development. This requires bridging molecular-scale predictions with process-scale models 287. Although progress has been made in several application areas (Sections 3.3 and 5.3.1) Multiscale integration represents the next critical frontier where materials informatics intersects with process systems engineering. This research domain would enable the co-optimized design of both materials and the processes that manufacture and deploy them, potentially unlocking efficiency gains inaccessible through sequential optimization of either domain alone. Table 4 summarizes the findings of this section.

7 Process Systems Engineering

7.1 Process and Product Design

Techniques such as Bayesian optimization 28, 288, 289, generative AI 290, 291, and reinforcement learning 292, 293 introduce new paradigms to leverage data to accelerate the exploration of complex design spaces and to generate new designs.

Process design is part art, part science — engineers draw on knowledge and creative insight to identify designs that fulfill different functions, and generating alternatives that are feasible from economic, environmental, and safety standpoints remains a persistent challenge. A critical first step is finding suitable representations (abstractions) of the design space to be explored. Digital representations have been proposed that capture process topology, relevant phenomena, and key properties (e.g., material flows, phase equilibria, chemical reactions) 294, 295, enabling the construction of process databases and the development of generative AI/ML models capable of proposing new designs 48, 296. As an example, 297 proposed a LLM for carbon capture and utilization.

This is analogous to how large language models use vast text corpora to generate new narratives: data representations of process structures define a language that AI/ML can use to generate novel alternatives. These capabilities can be further combined with rigorous process simulations and active learning to identify designs with desired characteristics. Key open challenges remain, however — capturing complex logic and expert intuition, and determining whether generative AI/ML can truly extrapolate beyond its training data to achieve genuine discovery rather than recombination.

Bayesian optimization (BO) has gained significant traction as a data-driven technique for process design, capable of optimizing both topology and operating conditions 28, 288, 289, 298. Unlike generative AI/ML, BO requires the user to more explicitly define the design space (e.g., via a superstructure of alternatives), but in return offers a principled framework for fusing experimental data with physical knowledge to steer design toward desired goals 31. This makes BO particularly valuable for experimentalists seeking to integrate process data with techno-economic and lifecycle performance evaluation. BO has also become a dominant paradigm in experimental and product design, with successful applications in solvent selection for extraction 299, electrolyte optimization for batteries 300, and product formulation 301. Despite these successes, handling discrete design decisions and high-dimensional spaces remains challenging. The PSE community has made meaningful progress here, proposing discrete kernel models 302, 303 and kernels that operate directly on graph and network structures 260, 31, 304.

In parallel, there has been growing interest in robust and safe BO for uncertainty-aware and safety-critical design. Robust BO explicitly accounts for parametric or environmental uncertainty, seeking designs that perform well under worst-case or risk-based conditions — exemplified by adversarially robust BO 305 and structure-exploiting frameworks such as BoFlex 306 and BONSAI 307, which target flexibility and networked process systems under uncertainty. Safe BO, by contrast, ensures that all evaluated designs remain within a safe operating region while gradually expanding it, as in SafeOpt 308 and domain-specific strategies such as safe explorative BO for plasma medicine. Together, these developments push BO beyond nominal optimization toward uncertainty-aware, safety-conscious frameworks better aligned with industrial practice.

Additional opportunities exist to leverage autoencoder models for mapping discrete decision spaces into continuous ones, enabling Bayesian optimization to conduct more effective searches. This approach has seen considerable use in molecular design, though its limitations remain poorly understood 44. A key — and sometimes underappreciated — insight from these studies is that AI/ML models inherently learn smooth, continuous latent representations from complex, high-dimensional input data. Graph convolutional neural networks, for instance, take an inherently discrete structure (a graph) and, through successive convolution operations, distill it into a continuous feature space. Transformer-based large language models similarly project discrete token representations into continuous embedding spaces. Central to this transformation is the use of probabilistic representations: variational autoencoders, for example, encode input data into a probabilistic latent space that is both continuous and structured, making it amenable to gradient-based optimization methods such as Bayesian optimization 44.

Significant open questions remain on how to learn latent representations that are easier for optimization models to navigate. The PSE community already implicitly exploits these capabilities by leveraging large language model architectures, but there is a clear need to tailor these tools to specific process and product design contexts. A particularly promising direction is using dimensionality reduction to help users visualize high-dimensional design spaces — molecular design has demonstrated this effectively, with visualizations that allow researchers to identify structural families and promising candidates 309, 310. Analogous tools for process design would be equally valuable: How similar or dissimilar are two designs? What families of designs exist? One could envision an interactive copilot that proposes candidates, visualizes trade-offs, and helps engineers navigate clusters of designs — moving beyond the single “optimal” solution. Such tools are beginning to emerge for chemical space exploration 311, and developing analogous systems for process structure spaces is a natural and important next step.

A further challenge lies in integrating established design tools — such as superstructure optimization — with AI/ML techniques. Superstructure optimization is a powerful paradigm that encodes all possible design alternatives and leverages mixed-integer programming to navigate combinatorial spaces without repetitive simulations. However, mixed-integer approaches struggle with the complex nonlinearities arising from detailed process phenomena. The PSE community has addressed this partly through surrogate modeling, replacing specific unit operations with mixed-integer linear representations 312, 313, 314, but surrogate construction itself requires data collection via rigorous simulations. Better integration and streamlining of simulation, surrogate modeling, and design optimization workflows remains an open need.

Despite significant advances that promise to transform how design tasks are conceived and executed, substantial challenges remain in making these tools effective for practitioners. Full automation of design is unlikely — nor is it the right goal. Instead, the field should strive to build tools that help engineers pose better questions, explore alternatives more efficiently and systematically, and quantify trade-offs and uncertainty in ways that are simply not possible today.

7.2 Process Control

Data-driven techniques have always been a key component of process control, from model discovery and controller tuning/learning, to state estimation, fault detection, and, more recently, accelerating the solution of control problems.

7.2.1 Learning dynamic models

Perhaps the most fundamental step in any controller design task is process modeling — constructing a model that predicts the dynamic behavior of the system. When the model structure is known, the task reduces to parameter estimation (system identification) 315, 316. When it is not, neural networks 317, 318, 319, 320, 321, 322, 323, 324, 325, 326 or Gaussian processes 327 can be used to learn approximate models. However, deep learning models lack interpretability, which limits trust in the safety-critical applications common in chemical engineering.

This has motivated sparse regression approaches 108, 328, 23, where basis functions are used to represent the dynamics. Beyond predictive accuracy, dynamic models learned from data must also preserve key system properties — stability, dissipativity, and relevant time scales. This has driven efforts to learn control-relevant structure directly from data, including dissipativity 329, 330, 331, Lyapunov functions 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, and Koopman operators 339, 340.

7.2.2 Learning and tuning controllers

Machine learning models have also been used to learn controllers from data. A classic example is reinforcement learning, in which a policy that maps the system’s state to a control action is learned to maximize a reward 341, 34, 292, 37. If the process model is known, one can use neural networks to parameterize and design the controller using standard control-theory as well as data-driven approaches 342. The dual task of learning controllers from data is that of learning observers. Observer design is a well-studied problem in process control 343, 344.

An alternative to data-driven controller design is to approximate control laws from data using supervised learning. A characteristic example is the approximation of MPC laws using neural networks 345, 346, 347 and decision trees 348, 349, as well as learning solution operators using Deep Neural Operators 350. These approaches learn a multiparametric mapping between the system state and the optimal control action, thereby overcoming the challenges of solving nonlinear optimization problems online. Recently, several data-driven approaches have been proposed that parameterize the observer via neural networks 351, 352, 353, 354.

Finally, ML has been used to tune controller parameters. For this task, the tuning is posed as a black box optimization problem and data-driven optimization techniques, such as Bayesian Optimization, can be used to optimize the black box function, i.e., control performance 355, 356.

7.2.3 Accelerating computation within MPC

Beyond surrogate modeling and policy learning, a newer direction utilizes ML to accelerate the solution algorithms used to solve optimal control problems 357. Here, ML models learn the behavior of the numerical method itself — specifically, how to tune solver hyperparameters for a given MPC instance. Applications include accelerating Benders decomposition for mixed-integer MPC by learning warm starts 358, approximating transition costs between operating points 359, selecting the best solution algorithm 358, 360, and choosing between centralized and distributed MPC architectures 361. Reinforcement learning has also been applied within Benders decomposition to navigate binary variable spaces 362 and to select the level of inexactness at each iteration 363.

These advances demonstrate that AI can accelerate MPC without compromising solution quality or stability guarantees. Notably, existing work focuses predominantly on mixed-integer MPC; extending ML-based tuning to nonlinear optimization solvers for continuous nonlinear MPC systems represents a promising open direction 364.

7.2.4 Learning the structure of optimal control problems

Learning approaches have also been applied to discover the structure of control problems using network science and statistical inference 365, 366, 367, 368, 369. In these methods, a control or optimization problem is represented as a graph encoding interaction patterns among variables and constraints, and has been used to uncover structure in dynamical systems 366, MPC problems 367, and general decision-making problems 365, 368, 369. A current limitation is that these approaches consider only structural interactions; extending them to account for functional interactions among variables could yield better decompositions, particularly when solution time is the primary performance criterion.

7.3 Supply Chain Planning, Scheduling, and Management

Supply chain networks in the chemical, energy, and bioprocess sectors are characterized by multi-tier structures consisting of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and end customers, interconnected through complex logistics and information flows. Global supply-chain disruption events, such as COVID-19 pandemic-related shutdowns, silicon wafer supply disruptions following the 2011 Japan tsunami, climate risks for sustainable biomass supply, supply chain shifts caused by the 2018 U.S. tariffs, growing cyber-security risks in globalized networks, and rising sustainability requirements have increased the need for planning approaches that are able to capture global disruptions and their effects across supply chains 370.

Early supply-chain models were built using transaction-focused approach that lacked coordination across functional domains, targeting cost efficiency within individual stages rather than system-wide performance 371. The best-value supply chains concept emphasizes a shift in supply-chain thinking from cost-focused, functionally segmented operations toward coordinated, system-wide performance optimization under multiple objectives, including responsiveness, flexibility, and alignment among partners 372. Much of the supply-chain modeling literature in 2000s was based on simplified modeling assumptions, including aggregated parameterizations and reduced network representations, often uses deterministic, single-stage, or single-echelon formulations to maintain tractability in large-scale supply-chain models 373, 374. While these approaches were well suited for earlier or highly aggregated supply-chain settings, they offer limited flexibility for supporting the agility, adaptability, and coordination required in today’s data-rich and time-varying environments.

AI/ML provide an opportunity for combining large-scale data analytics, probabilistic forecasting, and optimization-driven decision support 375, 1. Methods ranging from supervised learning to reinforcement learning, deep generative models, and digital-twin frameworks enable the characterization of complex causal relationships, rapid scenario evaluation, and self-optimizing operations. As organizations increasingly demand agility and resilience, ML offers the ability to react immediately to market fluctuations, changing customer preferences, transportation bottlenecks, and production disruptions. In the following subsections, we highlight several key AI/ML applications for supply chain planning, scheduling, and management.

7.3.1 Data-Driven Forecasting for Inventory, Procurement, and Demand Management

AI/ML methods have become widely used for demand, inventory, and procurement forecasting in modern supply chains. By capturing nonlinear relationships and complex temporal dynamics from high-dimensional data, ML techniques consistently outperform traditional statistical approaches and support more reliable demand planning 376, 377, contributing to lower inventory costs, reduced stockouts, and more stable production scheduling. Beyond forecasting, statistical learning methods such as principal component analysis have been applied to monitor inventory, demand, and logistics data streams, enabling early detection of anomalies and disruption risks in multi-echelon supply chains 378.

A variety of ML models — including multivariate regression, neural networks 379, and long short term memory networks LSTMs 380 — have been applied to demand and inventory forecasting, consistently outperforming baseline time-series methods across industrial settings 381 and improving both demand signal accuracy and operational resilience in logistics networks 382.

Kernel-based methods have proven effective when upstream procurement signals influence downstream demand; in the pharmaceutical sector, for instance, incorporating supplier shipment histories and production delays into forecasting models measurably improves accuracy 383. By anticipating shortages and disruptions before they propagate downstream, predictive analytics enables proactive risk mitigation and better sourcing decisions — highlighting ML’s broader role in capturing cause-and-effect relationships across supply chain tiers.

Beyond forecasting, data-driven optimization frameworks based on learned uncertainty information have been developed for decision modeling. For instance, Bayesian decision-support approaches have been proposed to incorporate incomplete performance data across economic, environmental, and social criteria using Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation, enabling robust supplier ranking and scenario analysis under data scarcity 384. Ning and You developed a data-driven adaptive robust optimization approach that applies principal component analysis and kernel density estimation to capture correlations and asymmetry in uncertainty data, enabling multi-stage planning decisions that adapt to uncertainty realizations 385. In this context, generative AI enables data-driven generation of demand and disruption scenarios for scenario-based analysis and decision support in supply-chain management 386.

Deep RL has also been applied to inventory decision-making. By using deep neural networks to learn dynamic and state-dependent decision policies, deep RL is well suited for sequential supply-chain problems under uncertainty. Deep RL can learn fully dynamic reorder policies for multi-echelon inventory systems, offering an alternative to find an optimal inventory policy under structural changes in the environment 387.

7.3.2 Dynamic Scheduling, Maintenance Planning, and Operational Optimization

In complex industrial systems, production scheduling and maintenance planning require fast adjustments in response to changing demand, equipment availability, and resource constraints. AI/ ML methods have therefore been increasingly adopted to support real-time, data-driven operational decision-making and reduce computational burden. In particular, surrogate modeling approaches have been used to approximate computationally expensive process models or mixed-integer scheduling formulations, enabling rapid evaluation of alternative production schedules and operating policies 388, 389, 390. Supervised learning has been integrated with mixed-integer programming to accelerate large-scale industrial scheduling decisions, as demonstrated in crude oil scheduling for coastal refineries with long-distance pipelines 391.

Beyond supervised learning approaches, reinforcement learning (RL) is particularly well suited to dynamic operating environments because it can learn adaptive decision policies for production sequencing, energy shifting, and inventory restocking under uncertainty. RL methods have been applied in process industries to manage competing operational targets and fluctuating resource availability 392. Deep RL has further been explored for chemical production scheduling by formulating the scheduling problem as a sequential decision-making process under uncertainty. Hubbs et al. developed a deep RL framework that enables online schedule generation in response to stochastic demand and losses from production condition changes 393. The method outperforms the mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) schedulers operating and having reasonable computational costs, showing the potential of real-time schedule optimization.

To facilitate the development and benchmarking of RL algorithms, the PSE community has also developed several representative benchmark environments, including OR-Gym 394, SafeOR-Gym 395, and PC-Gym 396. These platforms provide standardized environments for evaluating learning algorithms across a broad range of operations research and process systems engineering problems, thereby accelerating methodological development and reproducible performance comparisons.

From a PSE perspective, recent work highlights the importance of hybrid AI frameworks that tightly integrate data-driven learning with first-principles models and domain knowledge to enable safe, interpretable, and operationally feasible decision-making in process manufacturing systems 397. For instance, Burtea and Tsay proposed a constrained reinforcement learning framework that embeds known operational constraints directly into the action-selection process through optimization over learned value functions, ensuring feasibility and safety of inventory and operational decisions 38. Hybrid simulation-based optimization frameworks have also been applied to study centralized and decentralized decision-making in complex supply chains, capturing dynamic interactions and coordination effects under uncertainty 398, 399.

Predictive maintenance is another key application. ML models that learn equipment degradation patterns or failure probabilities allow maintenance to be scheduled before failures occur, reducing downtime and improving asset utilization. In chemical and energy systems, Q-learning and agent-based simulation frameworks have been explored for decentralized equipment control and failure-response actions 400.

7.3.3 Transportation, Routing, and Distribution Optimization

Transportation and warehousing activities relate to data such as vehicle movement data, shipment records, traffic information, and warehouse logs. Managing these complex and time-varying data series is crucial for improving routing efficiency, delivery reliability, and distribution planning. As a result, a variety of data-driven and learning-based methods have been developed to support decision-making in logistics networks.

Beyond traditional forecasting tasks, recent studies show that AI-based methods are increasingly used to support decision-making in transportation, logistics, and energy systems with sustainability goals. For example, AI models that combine neural networks with optimization techniques have been applied to analyze decarbonization options and operational trade-offs in industrial and maritime energy systems 401. In a recent perspective article, Kamkar et al. emphasize the growing role of AI in sustainable resource management, supply chain planning, and logistics optimization across chemical and energy sectors 402.

RL methods have been applied to dynamic vehicle routing, last-mile delivery, and multi-agent coordination, where agents learn adaptive decision policies that respond to uncertainty and time-varying operating conditions, which is challenging to represent with fixed rules in static optimization models 403.

When combined with digital supply chain twin frameworks, data-driven methods support the monitoring, simulation, and reconfiguration of transportation processes and logistics flows in response to disruptions, enabling improved visibility and resilience of distribution networks 404. Empirical studies in retail and parcel distribution report 10–15% transportation fuel reductions after adopting AI/ML-enhanced routing strategies 405.

7.3.4 Sustainable and Policy-Aware Supply Chain Design

In recent years, sustainability regulations and public policies such as carbon pricing, emissions caps, trade restrictions, and reporting requirements have influenced supply-chain design and operation. These policy constraints introduce additional uncertainty, nonlinearity, and multi-objective trade-offs that are difficult to represent using static or deterministic planning models.

AI/ML methods support policy-aware supply-chain decision-making by integrating regulatory constraints and sustainability metrics directly into data-driven optimization and control frameworks. Predictive models estimate policy-relevant variables (e.g., emissions), while prescriptive formulations incorporate these estimates into sourcing, production, transportation, and inventory decisions under regulatory limits. Reinforcement learning has been explored for policy-constrained operational control, enabling adaptive responses to mechanisms such as carbon trading or emissions caps while maintaining economic performance 406.

Beyond numerical optimization and traditional decision-making frameworks, as discussed in the previous section, LLMs have demonstrated strong capabilities in extracting and structuring information across many domains. Thus, LLMs may provide a new pathway for policy-aware supply-chain management by enabling the automated extraction, interpretation, and organization of regulatory texts and sustainability standards from unstructured reports. A recent work demonstrates the use of LLMs with mixed-integer optimization to support explainability, scenario exploration, and decision transparency in large-scale industrial supply chains 407.

7.3.5 Emerging AI Methods for Supply Chain Transformation

Emerging AI methods enable transformative advances in supply-chain planning, optimization, and operational decision support. Beyond developing accurate predictive models, modern AI-enabled PSE increasingly focuses on integrating these models into closed-loop decision-making frameworks that continuously adapt to changing operating conditions. These include: (i) predictive and prescriptive analytics, where predictive models estimate future system states (e.g., demand, supplier reliability) and prescriptive formulations such as MILP, mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP), or stochastic programming integrate ML-based forecasts to recommend optimal actions; (ii) digital twins, which create computational replicas of plants, logistics networks, or entire supply chains to evaluate “what-if” scenarios and test disruption responses, with ML accelerating validation and real-time updating 408; (iii) generative AI methods for scenario generation which provide demand trajectories, disruption scenarios, and multi-factor risk profiles to support robust stochastic optimization 409; (iv) RL for sequential decision-making, where agents learn policies for inventory management, operational control, production switching, or vehicle routing in dynamic environments; and (v) blockchain-enabled data governance, which enables decentralized, tamper-resistant data sharing across multi-stakeholder supply-chain networks. When combined with AI-driven analytics, blockchain-validated data enhance end-to-end supply-chain traceability, transparency, and strengthen trust 405. Together, AI/ML methods support the development of more adaptive, resilient, and data-driven supply-chain systems.

While these AI methods provide powerful predictive and optimization capabilities, their practical value depends on successful deployment within closed-loop PSE workflows. The lifecycle of AI-enabled decision-support systems typically begins with data acquisition from process sensors, enterprise databases, laboratory measurements, and supply-chain information systems, followed by data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model identification using statistical or machine-learning approaches. Developed models should then undergo rigorous validation and uncertainty quantification to ensure prediction reliability before being integrated with optimization, scheduling, and model predictive control frameworks for operational decision making 410 . Rather than remaining static offline models, AI systems should be continuously updated as new process and operational data become available to mitigate model drift and maintain predictive performance under changing operating conditions. Continuous monitoring of model accuracy, automated retraining strategies, and synchronization through digital twins further enable adaptive optimization and resilient real-time supply-chain management 411.

Despite rapid development, several factors may limit large-scale adoption of AI/ML in supply chains, including high data storage and processing costs, data-privacy and data-sharing constraints, organizational resistance to automation, and limited availability of high-quality data 412, 404. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated investments in data governance, workforce development, cross-functional alignment, and scalable digital facility. Beyond technical model development, successful industrial deployment also requires AI lifecycle management, including continuous model validation, uncertainty management, monitoring of model degradation, and mechanisms for periodic model updating. At the same time, growing supply chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions, and economic uncertainties underline the need for future supply chains to evolve toward more open, reactive, and robust structure where AI models operate as continuously updated components of integrated optimization and control systems rather than standalone predictive tools. Table 5 summarizes the findings of this section.

8 Industrial Applications of AI

Computational intelligence in industrial operations has evolved over several decades, progressing from first-principles expert systems to contemporary data-driven AI, and fundamentally reshaping how chemical manufacturing facilities operate, optimize, and innovate. Process companies increasingly view AI as their primary lever for the next wave of transformational gains in safety, reliability, and sustainability; British Petroleum, for example, has significantly improved production and reduced unplanned shutdowns through advanced AI analytics 413. This transformation, however, has been neither uniform nor complete, with some operational domains near-fully integrated while others remain largely untouched. In this section, we examine AI adoption across different operational levels and roles in process industry settings, exploring the heterogeneous adoption landscape, barriers to broader deployment, and the future trajectory of intelligent process systems.

8.1 Historical Evolution and Current State of AI/ML in Industrial Operations

Historically, high-fidelity first-principles models, such as CFD, finite element analysis, and kinetic modeling have been the workhorse of computational analytics in the process industry, enabling accurate simulation of complex “what-if” scenarios (Figure 2). However, their development remains time-consuming and requires specialized skills. This has spurred the adoption of AI/ML-based tools across operational domains, especially as ML algorithms, computing power, data infrastructure, and sensing capabilities have matured. The past several years have witnessed a meaningful “democratization” of AI/ML analytics: cloud infrastructure has made substantial computational resources accessible without major capital investment, open-source frameworks have lowered barriers to model development, and self-service platforms now enable process engineers with limited data science training to build, validate, and deploy models. This democratization has accelerated AI/ML adoption across multiple operational domains, though penetration depth remains highly uneven. Figure 2 shows the AI ML applications with the most penetration.

8.1.1 Current Mainstream Applications of AI/ML in Industrial Operations

Process control and monitoring represent the most mature application domain for AI/ML technologies in chemical plants 249. Historically, advanced process control (APC) systems have utilized techniques like FIR (finite-impulse response) and state-space modeling to build the model predictive controller (MPC). A recent trend is to move beyond traditional MPC implementations to incorporate advanced ML for better handling of process nonlinearities, adaptation to feedstock variations, and maintaining optimal operation across wide operating envelopes. These systems leverage techniques such as neural networks for nonlinear model identification 414, 415, 416 and reinforcement learning for adaptive control policy optimization 37, 417. Complementing advanced control, AI-based tools have become increasingly prevalent in process monitoring applications. Classical techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares (PLS) provide dimension reduction and fault detection in high-dimensional sensor spaces 418. Modern autoencoder neural networks learn compressed representations of normal operating conditions, with reconstruction errors serving as anomaly indicators 419. These monitoring systems serve as an early warning capability, detecting subtle deviations from normal operation before they escalate into process upsets, safety incidents, or product quality excursions.

Predictive maintenance (PdM) has emerged as another domain where AI/ML has achieved substantial industrial traction. The fundamental value proposition, transitioning from time-based preventive maintenance to condition-based strategies, has proven compelling across asset-intensive industries 420. ML models can absorb and integrate diverse, heterogeneous data streams including vibration signatures, thermal imaging, acoustic emissions, lubricant analysis, and process operating history to predict anomalous behavior 421, equipment degradation and forecast remaining useful life 422. Techniques ranging from random forests and gradient boosting for failure classification, to recurrent neural networks for time-series prediction of degradation trajectories have demonstrated significant economic value through reduced unplanned downtime, optimized maintenance resource allocation, and extended asset lifecycles 423. Companies like Shell 424 and Marathon Petroleum 425 have reported substantial reduction in unplanned outages using ML-based PdM solutions.

Virtual (or soft) sensors are an impactful application of ML, addressing the persistent challenge of obtaining physical measurements of critical process variables. Virtual sensors are implemented using neural networks, Gaussian process regression, or ensemble methods and are used to infer hard-to-measure variables such as product composition, reaction conversion, or catalyst activity from readily available temperature, pressure, and flow measurements 426. Recent advances in physics-informed ML modeling, which embed known physical constraints and conservation laws into ML algorithms, have significantly improved the extrapolation capabilities and physical consistency of these models 427.

Continuous process optimization is another important domain which is witnessing increasing AI adoption 428. Rather than periodic offline optimization studies followed by manual implementation of recommended operating conditions, modern real-time optimization (RTO) systems perform closed-loop optimization where machine learning models serve as surrogate representations of complex process economics and constraints 249. These surrogates enable rapid evaluation of alternative operating strategies and real-time optimization in response to changing feedstock properties, energy prices, and product demands.

8.1.2 Persona-based Applications

A critical insight that has emerged from both successful and failed AI/ML deployments in process industries concerns the necessity of persona-centric design. The recognition that plant operators, process engineers, maintenance personnel, and plant managers operate with different decision-making contexts, has profound implications for how AI/ML systems should be constructed and how their outputs should be presented. The governing principle of “delivering the right information, at the right time, to the right people” sounds deceptively simple but proves challenging to implement in practice.

Plant operators, who manage real-time process behavior and respond to disturbances and upsets, require AI/ML systems that provide immediate, actionable intelligence. Anomaly detection alerts must indicate not merely that a deviation has occurred, but what specific process variables are implicated and what operational interventions might address the issue. The critical requirement for operator-facing AI systems is transparency and explainability; operators must understand why a recommendation is being made and have confidence in the underlying reasoning.

Process engineers engage with AI/ML systems at a different level of abstraction. Their responsibilities encompass performance optimization, troubleshooting recurring issues, and continuous improvement of process operations. AI tools for this persona must support more sophisticated analyses: automated root cause analysis that systematically evaluates potential contributors to process upsets, full plant modeling capabilities that enable quantitative evaluation of proposed process modifications, and knowledge retrieval systems that surface relevant historical learnings from previous optimization studies or equipment failures. The temporal scale is longer (hours to weeks rather than seconds to minutes) and the emphasis shifts from reactive response to proactive improvement.

Plant managers require yet another perspective on plant operations. Their decisions concern resource allocation, production planning, and risk management. AI/ML systems serving this persona must aggregate operational data into strategic insights: performance dashboards that track key performance indicators against targets and historical trends, predictive analytics that forecast production capabilities and identify bottlenecks, and risk assessment frameworks that quantify exposure to various operational and market risks. The challenge lies in distilling the complexity of plant operations into concise, interpretable representations that support executive decision-making without overwhelming users with operational minutiae.

This persona-based architecture implies that a single monolithic AI system is unlikely to serve all stakeholders effectively. Rather, a layered information architecture is required where foundational AI capabilities related to predictive models, optimization engines, and knowledge bases are accessed through persona-specific interfaces and workflows that present information in forms appropriate to each user’s role, responsibilities and decision context.

8.1.3 Recent Trends

Real-time digital twins: While precise definitions tend to vary based on context, digital twins can be broadly viewed as virtual replicas 410 of any equipment, process, or entire plant. Real-time digital twins that can run in parallel to the physical assets provide unprecedented visibility into system-wide health status and efficiency. Moreover, high-fidelity digital twins that can be executed in real-time allow operators to evaluate potential control actions through what-if scenario analysis before implementation. However, owing to the challenges associated with developing a high-fidelity dynamic model whose behavior matches that of a physical plant, and which can be updated in real-time robustly with latest plant data, deploying comprehensive digital twins for complex processes still remain an aspirational target for many industries.

Nonetheless, the number of publicly reported successful digital twin applications is increasing; for example, Chevron 410 described how digital replicas of their plants are helping operators assess plant health in real-time. These digital twins invariably are hybrid in nature, wherein mechanism-driven first-principles equations are integrated with AI/ML techniques, resulting in computationally tractable models that are grounded in the physical realities of the underlying process.

Hybrid Modeling: The broader hybrid modeling technique underpinning these industrial digital twins spans many plant-scale case studies that illustrate its maturity. Sansana et al. surveyed hybrid modeling practice across the process industries in the context of Industry 4.0, cataloging architectures, tooling, and the challenges of embedding hybrid models within digital infrastructure at scale 411; the same group later showed that hybrid architectures can improve extrapolation and transfer learning when a process shifts to a new operating regime with only limited new data, using simulated biodiesel production as a case study 429. Shah et al. combined a deep neural network with a fermentation kinetic model to identify time-varying dependencies among kinetic parameters in an industry-scale (more than 100,000-gallon) fermenter, improving both accuracy and robustness relative to the mechanistic model alone 430 as an early example of the kind of plant-scale hybrid deployment envisioned above. Two recent reviews take a broader methodological view: Sharma and Liu classify hybrid approaches by whether ML complements first-principles science or science complements ML, spanning serial, parallel, and inverse hybrid architectures 431, while Schweidtmann et al. propose a more precise definition of hybrid model structures and revisit training methodologies in light of recent advances in physics-informed machine learning 432. A step-by-step tutorial by Shah et al. addresses the practical gap between these conceptual reviews and implementation, walking through the mathematical formulation and code-level construction of hybrid models for new practitioners 433. Early comparative work by Feyo de Azevedo et al. anticipated much of this industrial activity, established that hybrid mechanistic–neural-network structures can outperform either a purely mechanistic or a purely data-driven model on validation data using fed-batch fermentation as a benchmark case 434. Finally, at the kinetics scale underlying many of the reactor and catalytic applications discussed in Section 3, Pahari et al. combined machine learning with first-principles kinetic Monte Carlo simulation to define and predict “effective” activation energies on electrocatalyst surfaces that capture many-body adsorbate interactions absent from conventional kinetic models 435, illustrating that the same hybrid modeling paradigm extends from plant-wide digital twins down to the elementary reaction step.

Prescriptive analytics leverage AI/ML to not only predict future states but also recommend optimal actions for process improvement 436. Unlike descriptive and predictive analytics, which forecasts outcomes or flags potential equipment/process failures, prescriptive analytics recommends in real time the specific process interventions / maintenance actions that need to be taken to ensure safe and the most efficient operation in a given scenario. Specific solutions may involve usage of digital twins or ML algorithms that mine historical data to extract relevant process patterns to find optimal operational strategies.

8.2 Technical and Organizational Challenges to Widespread Adoption

Despite the demonstrated value of AI/ML applications in specific domains, widespread adoption across the process industries faces substantial challenges (Figure 3). Many AI/ML applications are still treated as “add-ons” rather than essential components of the process operation toolkit. These challenges encompass both technical and human factors that prove equally consequential for AI/ML adoption.

The “last-mile connectivity failure” phenomenon, where sophisticated AI systems are developed and deployed but fail to influence operational decisions, represents perhaps the most significant barrier to realizing value from AI/ML investments. Plant operators, the ultimate end-users of many AI systems, often express distrust of black-box recommendations, particularly from systems whose internal reasoning is opaque. Building trust requires AI systems that can explain their recommendations in terms operators understand, that demonstrate consistent reliability over extended periods, and that gracefully handle situations outside their training distribution by acknowledging uncertainty rather than offering spuriously confident/hallucinatory predictions.

“Dashboard fatigue” has emerged as a related challenge. Plant control rooms already feature numerous displays, alarm systems, and monitoring interfaces. The introduction of additional AI-powered dashboards, regardless of their analytical sophistication, often meets resistance from operators who view them as adding to information overload rather than reducing it. A commonly heard complaint is having too many dashboards to monitor, that reflects a deeper issue: the proliferation of isolated point solutions rather than integrated systems where different AI components communicate and coordinate. What operators need is not more information but better information, synthesized and presented in forms that directly support their decision-making rather than requiring them to integrate across multiple disconnected systems.

Platform fragmentation presents another systemic challenge. The current landscape features numerous specialized AI/ML tools and platforms, each addressing specific applications, such as optimization, digital twin, production scheduling, control, monitoring, predictive maintenance, quality prediction, but with limited interoperability. This fragmentation creates silos where insights generated by one system cannot inform decisions in another. A truly intelligent plant requires integration across these boundaries such that different AI components can communicate and coordinate; for example, predictive maintenance systems can inform optimization algorithms about impending equipment constraints, and anomaly detection systems can trigger automated root cause analysis workflows.

Model maintenance presents particularly vexing challenges that compound as AI/ML deployments scale across multiple applications and plant units. Machine learning models learn relationships from historical data reflecting specific operating conditions and equipment states, but when process behavior evolves, whether gradually through catalyst deactivation and heat exchanger fouling, or abruptly through equipment modifications or feedstock changes, model predictions drift from reality 416. The extrapolation inadequacy inherent in most machine learning methods becomes especially problematic when processes operate outside the historical training distribution, leading to inaccurate predictions or false alarms even when process behavior remains normal for new conditions. Determining when model updates are required, distinguishing genuine model degradation from transient disturbances, and ensuring retraining improves rather than degrades performance requires sophisticated diagnostics and often human judgment. Managing these tradeoffs at scale, across dozens or hundreds of models deployed throughout a plant or across multiple facilities, becomes daunting.

The model life cycle management in practice benefits from an explicit, repeatable framework rather than ad hoc intervention. Such a framework typically comprises: (i) continuous model monitoring, tracking input/output distributions, prediction residuals, and performance metrics against a validation baseline; (ii) automated drift detection, using statistical distance metrics (e.g., population stability index, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, or reconstruction error from an autoencoder trained on the reference distribution) to flag meaningful departure from the training domain; (iii) defined retraining triggers, specifying quantitative thresholds (sustained residual growth, drift-metric exceedance) at which retraining is initiated, rather than a fixed calendar schedule that may under- or over-correct; (iv) mandatory revalidation after known plant changes such as catalyst replacement, equipment modification, feedstock change must be treated as checkpoints independent of whether automated drift metrics have fired; (v) uncertainty-aware recommendations, so outputs carry calibrated confidence estimates and downstream decisions can be gated on that uncertainty; and (vi) governance that assigns clear ownership and approval authority for model updates in safety-critical applications, mirroring change-management practice already used for other safety-instrumented systems. Embedding these elements in the unified analytics platforms discussed above would let drift detected in one model (e.g., a soft sensor) automatically inform the retraining priority of downstream models (e.g., an RTO surrogate) that depend on it, rather than requiring independent, manually triggered maintenance across dozens of disconnected deployments.

The challenge of inadequate training data richness fundamentally limits the scope of achievable AI/ML applications, particularly for optimization and control applications requiring understanding of process behavior across broad operating envelopes. While chemical plants generate enormous data volumes, the vast majority accumulate during normal closed-loop operation where controllers maintain variables near setpoints, providing data valuable for monitoring applications but inadequate for optimization solutions requiring extensive coverage of the operating space. Models trained on such limited-excitation data may interpolate reasonably within narrow historical operating envelopes but fail when optimization algorithms suggest alternative strategies. The alternative of augmenting plant data with high-fidelity simulation-generated training data introduces substantial challenges: developing and maintaining comprehensive simulation models requires substantial engineering effort (often even more than training data-driven models) and ensuring models trained on simulated data perform reliably on actual plants remains nontrivial due to plant-model mismatch and unmeasured disturbances.

8.3 Large Language Models: A Paradigm Shift in Human-AI Interaction in Process Industry

Among the recent computational innovations, the one with potential for the most (constructive) disruption in industrial operations is the application of LLMs as “co-pilots” or “virtual assistants” to supplement the capabilities of plant operators and engineers. The claim is not that the LLMs will make existing AI applications obsolete, rather LLMs can help bring these AI applications closer to the end-users who are not proficient in advanced data analytics (as is the usual case in plant control rooms). Several commercial offerings are already appearing in this space 437, 438. Below are a few ways in which LLMs can help in the operational domain.

Generative AI can enable operators and engineers to interact with complex analytical systems through natural language, dramatically lowering the barrier to adoption. Rather than learning specialized software interfaces, users can ask questions, request analyses, and explore what-if scenarios using familiar conversational interactions. For example, a plant operator, upon detecting an unusual drift in a temperature signal, could ask in plain English, “which other signals are showing similar drifts as the reactor outlet temperature?” and the LLM can interface with an analytics tool to provide a direct answer supported with necessary visualizations. The operator could continue the conversation to further investigate and establish if the temperature drift is an isolated phenomenon indicating a potential sensor issue or a more serious process upset. Assuming that this interface can correctly reflect physical reality, the positive impact on operator productivity could be quite high.

The capability for contextual knowledge integration represents an equally significant advance. Large language models can in principle be fine-tuned or augmented through retrieval mechanisms to access plant-specific documentation, operating procedures, troubleshooting guidance, operator logbook entries, maintenance work-orders, equipment manuals, and historical incident reports. When combined with real-time process data and AI-generated insights, these systems can serve as intelligent assistants that provide contextualized guidance tailored to specific situations.

Conversational AI interfaces offer a potential solution to the aforementioned dashboard fatigue. Rather than presenting users with static displays that present information regardless of immediate relevance (a “push” model), conversational systems enable a “pull” mode of operation, where users request specific information as needed, in the form most useful for their current decision context. This shift from monitoring multiple parallel information streams to focused, query-driven information may prove more effective in supporting operational decision-making. The system becomes a collaborative partner that responds to expressed needs rather than a broadcasting station that demands continuous attention.

Knowledge transfer and retention of expert domain knowledge represent challenges that take on increasing urgency as experienced operators and engineers approach retirement. The accumulated wisdom (subtle indicators of equipment degradation, contextual factors affecting process behavior, troubleshooting heuristics developed over decades) resides largely in the tacit knowledge of personnel rather than in documented procedures. As opined by Baldea et al. 439, LLMs could utilize transcriptions of human conversations (e.g., among operators in an online meeting) as context for better decision making; the objective would be to be able to capture operational wisdom inherent in these plant control room discussions. Overall, this would closely emulate the way humans learn from each other. It is useful to distinguish two roles LLMs can play here, since they carry very different reliability requirements. As interfaces and orchestrators, LLMs translate natural-language requests into calls to existing, verified tools such as process historians, simulators, optimization solvers, validated analytics models and translate the results back into natural language; correctness remains the responsibility of the underlying tool, and the LLM’s role is interpretation and routing. As scientific or engineering reasoning engines, by contrast, LLMs are asked to perform the calculation, diagnosis, or design step themselves, drawing on patterns learned during pretraining rather than a verified computational tool. This second role is considerably riskier in process systems as LLMs carry no intrinsic guarantee of numerical accuracy, mass/energy-balance closure, or physical consistency, and can produce fluent, confident, and superficially plausible answers that are quantitatively wrong or cite nonexistent sources. LLM and agentic AI systems should, wherever possible, be restricted to the orchestrator role in operational settings connected to verified simulators, historians, and optimization tools, with a human-in-the-loop check before any recommendation is acted upon in a safety-critical decision. Recent multi-agent frameworks for process systems engineering illustrate this pattern, coupling LLM-based orchestration with specialized, verifiable computational agents rather than asking a single language model to reason end-to-end about plant behavior 56, 57.

Important caveats accompany these promising capabilities. Current LLMs can generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect responses (so-called hallucinations) which pose obvious risks in safety-critical process operations. The tendency of these models to exhibit a confident tone even when their knowledge base and information have high uncertainty, makes detecting unreliable outputs challenging.

8.4 Future Trajectory: Towards Increasingly Autonomous Operations

The evolution of AI/ML applications in process industries points toward several interconnected developments that collectively promise to move operations toward more autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent operations with synergistic human-machine collaboration. As previously discussed, LLM-based solutions are poised to spearhead human-machine collaboration. As far as autonomous operations (which entail utilization of new enabling technologies to automate some practically important tasks that have hitherto relied extensively on human intervention 439) are concerned, it is not far-fetched to speculate that in the near-to-medium term, the following technologies will become mainstream and help unleash the next wave of productivity gains.

Unified Data Analytics Platform

We previously discussed how operations personnel are flooded with siloed analytics solutions with fragmented data sources. Different areas of interest such as plant health and reliability, control, strategy, sustainability, optimization, albeit all correlated, have been approached individually and have their own solutions, often utilizing their own custom analytics infrastructure and rarely incorporating priorities beyond their own. There is a rejuvenated interest in the industry to move away from these custom, fragmented solutions toward unified platforms. A unified enterprise-wide platform and AI will allow a standardized way to access data across different solutions enabling a truly “intelligent” plant whose different components can communicate and coordinate. Achieving this level of integration requires not only technical standards for data exchange but also architectural frameworks that support loosely coupled systems with well-defined interfaces.

Reinforcement Learning (RL)-Based Adaptive Control

At the outset, the task of process control appears to be a mature task with established automation tools doing the bulk of the job (using classical PID controllers, MPCs, etc.). However, plant engineers will vouch for the daily challenges (due to tuning issues, creeping plant-model mismatch, etc.) they face in maintaining these systems and ensuring optimal controller performance over time. The successes of reinforcement learning in computational science augur well as a potential solution to this challenge wherein an automated RL agent continuously makes small interventions to the process to find optimal rewards and “learn” about the process environment on the fly to improve its actions. For example, Blum et al. investigated an RL controller at a Linde air separation plant and demonstrated a stable control behavior with superior control quality for over 20 days 440.
