Even with these advances, deploying reinforcement learning directly onto physical chemical plants remains difficult. This reality requires a more cautious perspective than simply assuming RL’s successes in other fields will easily translate here. Online exploration is frequently unsafe in safety-critical settings, historical data often lack sufficient variation (Section 8.2), and it is hard to guarantee closed-loop stability or constraint satisfaction once a policy moves beyond its training data. These algorithms typically require thousands to millions of environment interactions to converge, which is computationally expensive. Researchers are pursuing three complementary strategies to address these hurdles. Safe RL methods limit the exploration or action space itself through chance-constrained formulations or action-projection layers, ensuring that only feasible actions are ever applied to the plant 292, 37. Offline RL avoids the risks of online exploration altogether by training policies entirely on historical or simulated data; recent studies have shown this works for chemical reactor control by pairing an offline policy with a real-time safety layer that corrects actions using a learned cost model 441. Embedding prior knowledge of system dynamics and hard constraints directly into the learning loop is a promising route to reduce this burden. For example, RL-assisted MPC architectures constrain the RL agent’s search to actions that a model-based controller has already deemed feasible, 442 This hybrid setup drastically lowers the sample complexity compared to model-free RL baselines and enables faster convergence during training while maintaining robust constraint satisfaction. RL-based adaptive PID controller tuning solutions have also been proposed 443. Across all these strategies, the most persistent challenge is bridging the simulation-to-plant gap. Policies developed on simplified or first-principles simulators often underperform on real equipment because of unmodeled dynamics and plant-model mismatch. For now, RL is not a replacement for MPC but a very valuable addition to MPC and other established control strategies in safety-critical chemical processes.

Digital Twin Integration

Comprehensive digital twins that combine first-principles models, data-driven surrogates, and real-time optimization will enable true predictive operations and not just anticipating failures, but proactively adjusting operations to prevent issues before they manifest. Real-time digital twins running in parallel to their physical counterparts and “keeping” a check on the behavior of the actual operation would help avoid “surprise” plant upsets leading to costly plant trips. With the digital twins as components of the unified analytics platform, certain well-characterized operational regimes may become fully autonomous, with AI systems managing startups, shutdowns, and transitions while human operators focus on higher-level supervision and handling of off-normal situations.

Holistic Closed-Loop Plant-Wide Optimization

Process optimization is a computationally expensive task, with large complexes often broken down into smaller units for optimization purposes. Or, in a common industrial setting, MPC keeps operations at optimal control points, with optimal setpoints coming down from the RTO layer. Often, the models used by MPC and RTO layers are different, resulting in potentially sub-optimal operations especially during fast-paced process transitions. However, ongoing computational innovations 444, development of ML-enabled digital twins, and setup of unified analytics platforms raise hope for a future where large complexes can be holistically optimized as an integrated system balancing process mode variations, product demand fluctuations, and aging equipment. Table 6 summarizes the findings of this section.

9 Conclusions

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have transitioned from niche analytical tools to foundational components of modern chemical engineering research and practice. This review has surveyed recent advances across length and time scales, from atomistic simulations and materials discovery to process systems engineering and industrial operations, highlighting both transformative successes and persistent challenges. Collectively, the contributions reviewed here demonstrate that the impact of AI/ML in chemical engineering is no longer speculative: it is measurable, growing, and increasingly indispensable.

A central theme emerging across all application domains is the shift from purely data-driven models toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks. As emphasized in the Introduction, chemical engineering problems are constrained by mass, energy, momentum, and thermodynamic laws, and successful AI/ML models increasingly reflect this reality. Physics-informed neural networks, hybrid mechanistic–data-driven models, thermodynamically consistent learning architectures, and structure-preserving control models illustrate how embedding physical structure improves predictive accuracy, interpretability, extrapolation behavior, and safety. These developments directly address long-standing concerns about black-box learning in safety-critical and extrapolative regimes.

At the molecular and materials scales, machine-learned interatomic potentials, graph neural networks, and generative models have dramatically expanded the accessible design space for catalysts, adsorbents, membranes, and functional materials. By enabling close to ab initio accuracy at orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost, these models have accelerated materials screening, enabled inverse design, and facilitated autonomous discovery platforms that combine computation and experimentation. Symmetry-aware and equivariant architectures have improved data efficiency and physical fidelity, while benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation protocols have strengthened reproducibility and promoted community-wide, collaborative progress.

At the process unit and plant scales, AI/ML methods have enhanced multiscale simulation, optimization, and control. Learning-based surrogates and structure-discovery methods now complement traditional first-principles approaches, enabling real-time optimization, adaptive experimentation, and closed-loop operation. In process systems engineering, Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning, and generative models offer new paradigms for design, scheduling, and supply-chain management under uncertainty. When integrated with first-principles constraints, these approaches retain feasibility and interpretability while enabling rapid exploration of complex decision spaces.

Industrial deployment highlights both the promise and the limits of current AI/ML technologies. Applications in process monitoring, predictive maintenance, soft sensing, and optimization have delivered tangible value, yet challenges remain in last-mile adoption, model lifecycle management, trust, and organizational integration. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) as interfaces and copilots represents a qualitative shift in human–AI interaction, with the potential to reduce cognitive load, mitigate dashboard fatigue, and democratize access to advanced analytics. However, ensuring factual grounding, uncertainty awareness, and safe operation remains essential for their use in industrial environments.

Looking forward, several research imperatives stand out. These include: (i) deeper integration of conservation laws, thermodynamics, and stability guarantees into learning architectures; (ii) robust uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution detection for safe decision-making; (iii) scalable multiscale frameworks that bridge materials discovery with process-level performance; (iv) unified, interoperable platforms that support coordinated analytics across the enterprise; and (v) explicit, enforced standards for computational reproducibility, including public release of code, preprocessing and featurization scripts, data splits, trained model parameters, hyperparameters and tuning procedures, random seeds, and software/environment versions. On this last point, we echo the emerging norms of adjacent computational disciplines and journals and argue that chemical engineering AI/ML research, and the journals that publish it, should move toward comparable minimum requirements: the current inconsistency in code and data availability has repeatedly forced independent researchers to spend substantial effort reimplementing or guessing at published workflows, and it undermines fair comparison of reported performance across studies. Progress along these dimensions will determine whether AI/ML evolves from a powerful set of tools into a truly enabling infrastructure for chemical engineering, and will be further supported by (vi) expanding availability of open-source data sets.

We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. The most successful approaches respect physical laws, leverage domain knowledge, and place human expertise at the center of the decision-making loop by providing the correct level of information for the context. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding will be essential to realizing their full potential across research and industrial practice.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
